Presentation comparisons and their explicit homotopies are proved in F.11. No compatible choice of the individual contracting homotopies is needed for the induced homology maps.

Tensor commutes with this colimit term by term: a tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors, and each coefficient has a common-stage representative; its balancing relations and equalities hold at a later stage. The right side has colimit $\operatorname{NL}_{U^{-1}B/A}$ by the complete canonical-presentation proof F.24.

Finally filtered colimits commute with homology here. A cycle in either colimit has a stage representative; its differential is zero at some later stage, giving a cycle there. If its homology class vanishes, it is the differential of a representative vector in the colimit. Put the two representatives and their equality at one common successor to obtain a boundary there. This proves both directions of the homology-colimit isomorphism. The stage maps induce isomorphisms in degrees one and zero, so their colimit does too. All other homology groups vanish since these complexes have only two terms. This proves the claimed quasi-isomorphism, without a Noetherian or finite-generation hypothesis on $U$. The zero localization is included in the same diagrams. ∎

Lemma F.66: localize relative complete intersection

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 00ST.

Let $R$ be Noetherian and put $S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$. In each situation below there are $g\in S$ and a polynomial lift $h$ of $g$ for which $$S_g=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n,T]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,hT-1)$$ is a relative global complete intersection as defined in F.4.

  1. If every nonempty fibre over $V(I)$, for an ideal $I\subset R$, has dimension $n-c$, one may require $g\equiv1\pmod{IS}$.
  2. If the fibre over $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$ has dimension $n-c$, one may require the image of $g$ in that fibre to be a unit.
  3. If a point $\mathfrak q$ of the fibre over $\mathfrak p$ has fibre point-dimension $n-c$, one may require $g\notin\mathfrak q$.

Proof. Set $d=n-c$. The neighbourhood bound proved in F.39 gives, around every point whose fibre point-dimension is at most $d$, a principal neighbourhood on which every fibre point-dimension is at most $d$. The union of these neighbourhoods is an open $W$ with that same bound. Each of its nonempty fibres has dimension at most $d$: a finite-type field fibre is Noetherian, and its component dimensions are its point-dimensions at the corresponding generic points, as in F.20. Open subsets retain this bound.

In case (1) choose $W$ containing $V(IS)$; each point of those fibres has point-dimension at most their assumed dimension. Write the closed complement of $W$ as $V(J)$ in $\operatorname{Spec}S$. The equality $V(J+IS)=\varnothing$ implies $J+IS=S$: a proper ideal would be contained in a maximal, hence prime, ideal. Write $1=g+b$ with $g\in J$ and $b\in IS$. Then $g\equiv1\pmod{IS}$, and $D(g)\subset W$.

In case (2) take $W$ containing the entire indicated fibre, and again write its complement as $V(J)$. If $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, the image ideal $J(S\otimes_R k)$ is the unit ideal. Choose a finite expression $1=\sum_j\beta_j\bar g_j$, where $g_j\in J$. Each $\beta_j$ is represented in $S_{R\setminus\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pS_{R\setminus\mathfrak p}$. Clear their finitely many denominators to obtain $b_j\in S$ and $s\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ with $\beta_j=\bar b_j/\bar s$. Thus $g=\sum_j b_jg_j\in J$ has fibre image $\bar s$, a unit. Again $D(g)\subset W$.

In case (3), one of the principal neighbourhoods supplied directly by F.39 is $D(g)$ with $g\notin\mathfrak q$ and the required upper bound. In all three cases select any polynomial lift $h$ of $g$. Adjoining the inverse of $h$ gives the presentation in the statement, by the explicit substitution $T\mapsto g^{-1}$ and its inverse. Every nonempty fibre of this presentation has dimension at least $$ (n+1)-(c+1)=d.$$ Indeed, in its polynomial ring over the residue field a minimal prime over $c+1$ equations has height at most $c+1$, by AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.1; AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3 gives that component dimension as $n+1$ minus its height. The upper bound on $D(g)$ makes the dimension exactly $d$. This proves the relative global complete-intersection assertion, without presupposing flatness; its flatness is subsequently proved in F.77. Empty fibres impose no dimension test, and a zero localization is included. ∎

Lemma F.67: locally smooth

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 00TC.

For any ring map $R\to S$, smoothness is equivalent to the existence, around every prime of $S$, of a principal localization that is smooth over $R$.

Proof. Use the finite-presentation and cotangent-complex definition F.6. If $S/R$ is smooth, then $S_g$ is finitely presented by adjoining an inverse variable. The exact calculation F.72, together with the presentation comparison F.11, identifies its conormal complex with the localized complex plus a contractible summand. Its first homology is zero and its differential module is the localization of a finite projective module. Localization keeps the splitting of a finite free module, so that module is still finite projective. Thus $S_g/R$ is smooth.

For the converse, the elements defining the given neighbourhoods generate the unit ideal: otherwise a maximal ideal containing them would be an uncovered prime. A finite expression for $1$ gives a cover by $D(g_1),\ldots,D(g_r)$. The complete gluing proof F.35 makes $S/R$ finitely presented. Fix $S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/I$ with $I$ finite. For this presentation set $$K=\ker(I/I^2\xrightarrow{d}S^n),\qquad M=\operatorname{coker}(I/I^2\xrightarrow{d}S^n)=\Omega_{S/R}.$$ The derivatives of a finite list generating $I$ generate the image of $d$, so $M$ is finitely presented. Exact localization and F.72/F.11 identify $K_{g_i}$ with the zero first homology of each smooth chart. The power-annihilator module calculation in F.35 therefore gives $K=0$.

It remains to produce a global projective splitting for $M$. Write $\pi:S^n\twoheadrightarrow M$. On each chart $M_{g_i}$ is finite projective. A section $s_i$ of $\pi_{g_i}$ exists: write that projective module as a summand of a finite free module, lift the free basis through $\pi_{g_i}$, and restrict the resulting lift to the summand.

For a finitely presented module, localization of $\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,S^n)$ is $\operatorname{Hom}_{S_{g_i}}(M_{g_i},S_{g_i}^n)$. Indeed a finite presentation of $M$ identifies both modules with the kernel of the same matrix between finite powers of $S^n$, and localization is exact. Clear the denominator of $s_i$ to obtain $t_i:M\to S^n$ whose localized composite is $g_i^{a_i}1_M$. The error $\pi t_i-g_i^{a_i}1_M$ vanishes on a finite generating list after localization. A further common power of $g_i$ kills those finitely many errors. After multiplying $t_i$ by that power, we have an actual equality $$\pi t_i=g_i^{e_i}1_M.$$ Increase $e_i$ to a positive integer if needed. These powers generate $1$: expand a finite unit expression in the $g_i$ to exponent $1+\sum_i(e_i-1)$; every monomial contains one of the required powers. Choose $c_i$ with $\sum_i c_ig_i^{e_i}=1$. Then $t=\sum_i c_it_i$ satisfies $\pi t=1_M$. Thus $S^n=t(M)\oplus\ker\pi$, with both summands generated by projections of its finite basis. This proves finite projectivity of $M$ directly.

We have proved finite presentation, zero first cotangent homology and finite projective differentials, exactly F.6. If $S=0$, its finite presentation is $R/(1)$ and both cotangent modules are zero, so the conclusion also holds for the empty spectrum. No Noetherian hypothesis is needed. ∎

Lemma F.68: make etale map prescribed residue field

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 41287–41319.

Let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime of a ring $R$, and let $L/\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ be finite separable. There are a finitely presented étale $R$-algebra $R'$ and a prime $\mathfrak p'$ over $\mathfrak p$ with an isomorphism $\kappa(\mathfrak p')\cong L$ respecting the given residue-field extension.

Proof. Choose a finite field-generating list $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ for $L/\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, for example a vector-space basis. Put $E_0=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and $E_i=E_{i-1}(\alpha_i)$. Each step is finite separable: the minimal polynomial over $E_{i-1}$ divides a separable polynomial over $E_0$ and therefore has no repeated root.

Inductively construct a finitely presented étale $R$-algebra $A_i$ with a prime $\mathfrak q_i$ and a compatible identification $\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)=E_i$. Start with $A_0=R$ and $\mathfrak q_0=\mathfrak p$. Suppose the preceding stage is constructed, and write $A=A_{i-1}$, $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak q_{i-1}$. Let $$\bar F_i(T)=T^{e_i}+\sum_{j<e_i}\bar a_jT^j\in E_{i-1}[T]$$ be the monic minimal polynomial of $\alpha_i$. The residue map $A_{\mathfrak q}\to E_{i-1}$ is surjective, so lift each $\bar a_j$ as a fraction $a_j/s_j$ with $s_j\notin\mathfrak q$. The product $h=\prod_j s_j$ is outside $\mathfrak q$, and all these lifts belong to the single principal localization $A_h$. They give a monic polynomial $F_i\in A_h[T]$. Set $$A_i=(A_h[T]/(F_i))_{F_i'}.$$ Its defining equation has an invertible derivative. The full one-equation square-zero correction AG-CA-17, Proposition 6.1 makes this map étale. Principal localization is formally étale by its Theorem 1.2 and finitely presented by its inverse-variable equation. Finite composition, with the equation substitution proof F.28, therefore makes $A_i/R$ finitely presented and étale.

Evaluation at $T=\alpha_i$ defines a ring map $A_i\to E_i$: its derivative has nonzero value by separability, so its inverse can be evaluated. Let $\mathfrak q_i$ be the kernel. It is prime, and its contraction to $A$ is exactly $\mathfrak q$, since the restriction is the given residue map and $h$ has nonzero residue.

To compute its residue field, let $D_i$ be the image of $A_i$ in $E_i$. It is a domain, and $A_i/\mathfrak q_i=D_i$. The fraction field of the image of $A_h$ is $E_{i-1}$: this image is $(A/\mathfrak q)_h$, and localization does not change its fraction field $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. Thus $\operatorname{Frac}D_i$ contains $E_{i-1}$ as well as $\alpha_i$, and so contains $E_i=E_{i-1}(\alpha_i)$. It lies inside $E_i$, giving equality. Localization at the kernel identifies $$\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)=\operatorname{Frac}(A_i/\mathfrak q_i) =\operatorname{Frac}D_i=E_i.$$ This uses the fraction field of the image; it does not require the evaluation map itself to be onto the field.

Continue through the finite tower. Taking $R'=A_r$ and $\mathfrak p'=\mathfrak q_r$ gives the required extension and prime, with all residue identifications commuting with the original map from $R$. For the trivial extension the empty tower gives $R'=R$ and $\mathfrak p'=\mathfrak p$. ∎

Lemma F.69: make separably generated

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 10182–10253.

For any finitely generated field extension $K/k$, there is a commutative square of inclusions $$ \begin{array}{ccc} K&\longrightarrow&K'\\ \uparrow&&\uparrow\\ k&\longrightarrow&k' \end{array} $$ in which $k'/k$ and $K'/K$ are finite purely inseparable and $K'/k'$ is separably generated.

Proof. Choose a finite field-generating list and a maximal algebraically independent sublist $T_1,\ldots,T_d$. Every remaining generator is algebraic over $F=k(T_1,\ldots,T_d)$: a polynomial dependence using that generator has a nonzero coefficient after substituting the independent $T_j$. A finite algebraic generator tower is finite. At each step, division by the monic minimal polynomial gives a power basis; multiplication of these bases gives a basis of the whole tower, since grouping a relation by the powers of the last generator proves independence inductively. Thus $K/F$ is finite. In characteristic zero its irreducible polynomials have nonzero derivatives, so every tower step is separable. The entire separable-tower proof AG-CA-17, Lemma 7.1 gives the result with $k'=k$ and $K'=K$.

Assume now characteristic $p>0$. We first prove the finite-extension facts used in the construction. For a finite extension $E/F$, the elements separable over $F$ form a subfield $E_s$. Indeed if $x,y$ are separable, the minimal polynomial of $y$ over $F(x)$ divides its separable polynomial over $F$. The two separable steps and the same complete separable-tower proof make every element of $F(x,y)$ separable over $F$. This proves closure under sums, products and inverses. As a subspace of the finite-dimensional $F$-space $E$, this field is finite over $F$.

If $x\in E$ has irreducible minimal polynomial $f$, repeatedly remove zero derivatives to write $$f(X)=g(X^{p^e}),\qquad g'\ne0.$$ This process terminates as degrees decrease; $g$ is irreducible because a factorization would substitute to one of $f$. Its derivative has smaller degree, so the Euclidean algorithm gives $\gcd(g,g')=1$. Hence $x^{p^e}$ is separable over $F$ and lies in $E_s$. A common exponent for a finite field-generating list makes every $p^e$th power from $E$ belong to $E_s$: apply Frobenius to its rational expressions. Thus $E/E_s$ is purely inseparable.

We will use the degree calculation without an external $p$-basis result. If $\beta^p\in H$ but $\beta\notin H$, its minimal polynomial over $H$ divides $X^p-\beta^p=(X-\beta)^p$ in a field containing $\beta$. A monic proper nonconstant factor of degree $r<p$ has coefficient $-r\beta$ at degree $r-1$. Since $r$ is nonzero in the field, a factor over $H$ would force $\beta\in H$, a contradiction. The minimal polynomial therefore has degree $p$. By adjoining the powers of each purely inseparable generator in reverse order, starting from a power in the base, each nontrivial step has this degree. Multiplication of the power bases shows that every finite purely inseparable degree is a power of $p$.

Apply these facts to $K/F$, and call its separable subfield $K_s$. Prove the desired assertion by strong induction on $m=[K:K_s]$, for all finitely generated extensions with their chosen transcendence bases. If $m=1$, the chosen $T_j$ already separate $K/k$. If $m>1$, choose $x\in K\setminus K_s$ and the least $e\geq1$ with $x^{p^e}\in K_s$. Put $$\beta=x^{p^{e-1}},\qquad \alpha=\beta^p\in K_s.$$ Then $\beta\notin K_s$. The degree calculation gives $[K_s(\beta):K_s]=p$ and $[K:K_s(\beta)]=m/p$.

Let $$P(X)=X^n+\sum_{i<n}a_iX^i\in F[X]$$ be the separable minimal polynomial of $\alpha$. Write all $a_i$ as rational functions in $T$, and list the finitely many coefficients of $k$ occurring in their numerators and denominators. Adjoin their $p$th roots compatibly over $K$, one at a time. Such a root exists in a field extension: take the quotient by an irreducible factor of $X^p-c$. The quotient is a field by the Euclidean algorithm. A root is unique in any common extension, since $(u-v)^p=u^p-v^p$. All old fields therefore remain embedded in these successive root fields. Let $k_1$ be the field generated by these roots over $k$. It is finite purely inseparable, and $k_1^p\subset k$, since taking the $p$th power of any rational expression puts all its coefficients and generators in $k$.

In the same compatible extension adjoin $U_j$ with $U_j^p=T_j$. They are algebraically independent over $k_1$: a nonzero polynomial relation would, after taking its $p$th power, be a nonzero relation among the $T_j$ over $k$. Its coefficients remain nonzero under Frobenius. Put $$F_1=k_1(U_1,\ldots,U_d),\qquad L=KF_1.$$ This gives the actual commuting intermediate field square. The extension $L/K$ is finite and purely inseparable; it adjoins finitely many roots with $p$th powers in $K$. The $p$th power of any rational expression in them lies in $K$.

Take coefficientwise $p$th roots of the chosen numerator and denominator for each $a_i$, and substitute the $U_j$. This gives $b_i\in F_1$ with $b_i^p=a_i$. The denominator is nonzero because its $p$th power is the original nonzero denominator. Define $$Q(X)=X^n+\sum_{i<n}b_iX^i,\qquad Q(X)^p=P(X^p).$$ Then $Q(\beta)^p=P(\alpha)=0$, so $Q(\beta)=0$. The derivative calculation, using $i^p=i$ in the prime field, gives $$Q'(\beta)^p=P'(\alpha)\ne0.$$ Write $Q=hq$ with $h$ the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ over $F_1$. Evaluation of $Q'=h'q+hq'$ at $\beta$ implies $h'(\beta)q(\beta)\ne0$. Thus $h$ is separable, and $\beta$ is separable over $F_1$.

Every separable polynomial remains square-free after a field extension: its Euclidean identity with its derivative remains an identity equal to one after extending coefficients. The minimal polynomial of a generator after base change divides that polynomial and is therefore separable too. A finite generating tower for $K_s/F$ consequently gives a separable tower for $K_sF_1/F_1$. The minimal polynomial of the now separable $\beta$ over this larger field divides its separable polynomial over $F_1$, so this final step is separable as well. The separable-tower proof gives $$H=K_s(\beta)F_1\subset L_s,$$ where $L_s$ denotes the separable subfield of the finite extension $L/F_1$.

To bound its remaining inseparable degree, take a basis of $K$ over $K_s(\beta)$ of size $m/p$ and span it over $H$ inside $L$. This span contains $K$ and $H$, contains one, and is closed under multiplication, since the basis-product coefficients belong to $K_s(\beta)\subset H$. It is a finite-dimensional domain over $H$, hence a field: nonzero multiplication is injective, therefore surjective, and supplies an inverse. It contains $F_1$ and $K$, so equals $L$. Consequently $$[L:L_s]\leq[L:H]\leq m/p<m.$$ Also $L/F_1$ is finite, by the same spanning argument starting with a basis of $K/F$. The $U_j$ are a transcendence basis for the finitely generated extension $L/k_1$. Strong induction thus applies to this precise new data, giving finite purely inseparable $k_2/k_1$ and $L'/L$ with $L'/k_2$ separably generated.

Finally finite purely inseparable extensions compose: for each element of $L'$, a $p$-power lies in $L$ and a further $p$-power lies in $K$. The same argument applies to $k_2/k$. Finiteness follows by multiplying their finite tower degrees. Taking $K'=L'$ and $k'=k_2$ gives the asserted square. Empty transcendence bases, trivial adjunctions and the base case are all included. ∎

Lemma F.70: matrix left inverse

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07DQ.

Let \(A\) be an \(n\times m\) matrix over a commutative ring \(R\), where \(0\leq m\leq n\), and let \(J\) be the ideal of its maximal minors. Every \(f\in J\) has an \(m\times n\) matrix \(B\) with \(BA=f1_m\). Conversely, existence of such a \(B\) implies \(f^m\in J\).

Proof. For an increasing \(m\)-element subset \(I\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(E_I\) select those coordinates from \(R^n\), and put \(A_I=E_IA\). Its determinant is the corresponding minor. By the complete cofactor calculation in F.19, \[ \operatorname{adj}(A_I)E_IA=(\det A_I)1_m. \] Thus, from an expression \(f=\sum_I c_I\det A_I\), the finite sum \[ B=\sum_I c_I\operatorname{adj}(A_I)E_I \] constructs the required matrix.

For the converse, here is the determinant product calculation. Expand each column of \(BA\) as the linear combination of columns of \(B\) whose coefficients are entries of that column of \(A\). Multilinearity follows directly from the determinant permutation formula. A term choosing the same column twice is zero by the equal-column cancellation. For any fixed set \(I\) of distinct chosen columns, order those indices increasingly. Reordering them in all possible ways contributes their permutation signs; the signed sum of their coefficient products is exactly \(\det A_I\). The remaining column determinant is \(\det B^I\), where \(B^I\) uses the columns indexed by \(I\). Consequently \[ \det(BA)=\sum_{|I|=m}(\det B^I)(\det A_I)\in J. \] When \(BA=f1_m\), its determinant is \(f^m\). This proves the converse over arbitrary rings, including rings with nilpotents. If \(m=0\), the sole minor is the empty determinant \(1\), so \(J=R\). The unique map to and from the zero module supplies the first assertion, and \(f^0=1\in J\) supplies the second. ∎

Lemma F.71: presentation sym exterior

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 00DO. The quotient maps and both kernels are proved below.

For an exact sequence \(M_2\xrightarrow{u}M_1\xrightarrow{v}M\to0\) of modules over any commutative ring and every integer \(n\geq1\), there are exact sequences \[ M_2\otimes_R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-1}M_1 \longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^nM_1 \longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^nM\longrightarrow0, \] \[ M_2\otimes_R\bigwedge^{n-1}M_1 \longrightarrow\bigwedge^nM_1 \longrightarrow\bigwedge^nM\longrightarrow0. \] The first maps multiply, respectively wedge, with \(u(x)\); the second maps apply \(v\) to every factor. In degree zero both second maps are the identity of \(R\), so both kernels are zero.

Proof. Put \(N=\operatorname{im}u\), so exactness identifies \(M=M_1/N\). Construct the tensor algebra \(T(M_1)=\bigoplus_{d\geq0}M_1^{\otimes d}\) with multiplication by concatenation. Balancing in each tensor factor makes that product well defined. Its symmetric quotient imposes \(xy=yx\) for degree-one generators; its exterior quotient imposes \(x^2=0\) for every degree-one generator. In the latter quotient, expanding \((x+y)^2=0\) gives \(xy=-yx\) over every ring, including characteristic two.

In either algebra let \(L\) be the two-sided homogeneous ideal generated by the degree-one image of \(N\). The factorwise map to the corresponding algebra of \(M_1/N\) is onto: every pure tensor in the target lifts, and pure tensors generate each degree. It kills \(L\). Its inverse on the quotient is explicit. Send a class \(\bar x\in M_1/N\) to the class of any lift \(x\) in the source algebra modulo \(L\). Another lift differs by an element of \(N\), hence gives the same class. This map is linear, so its products extend to the tensor algebra by the tensor balancing relations. Those products obey commutation, respectively square-zero, relations in the indicated quotient; it therefore descends to the symmetric, respectively exterior, algebra. The two composites fix every degree-one generator and the scalar ring, hence every product and sum of generators. They are inverse graded algebra maps.

It remains to identify the degree-\(n\) part of \(L\). It is spanned by products having one selected factor in \(N\), since those generate the ideal and all factors have nonnegative degree. In the symmetric case move that factor to the front by commutation. In the exterior case move it to the front using \(xy=-yx\), retaining the resulting sign. Every remaining product has degree \(n-1\). Thus that part is exactly the image of \(N\otimes_R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-1}M_1\), respectively \(N\otimes_R\bigwedge^{n-1}M_1\), under multiplication. Each selected element of \(N\) lifts through \(u\), so these are also the images of the stated maps from \(M_2\). The inverse quotient maps just constructed prove that these images are exactly the kernels. The ideal has no degree-zero part, proving the separate degree-zero assertion. No module is assumed finite or free. ∎

Lemma F.72: principal localization NL

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37031–37116.

Let $A\to B$ be a ring map, $g\in B$, and $P\twoheadrightarrow B$ a polynomial presentation over $A$ with kernel $I$. Choose $f\in P$ mapping to $g$. The map $P[X]\to B_g$ extending the presentation and sending $X$ to $g^{-1}$ has kernel $J=(I,fX-1)$, and:

  1. $J/J^2\cong(I/I^2)_g\oplus B_g[fX-1]$.
  2. $\Omega_{P[X]/A}\otimes_{P[X]}B_g\cong(\Omega_{P/A}\otimes_PB_g)\oplus B_g\,dX$.
  3. The two-term conormal complex is isomorphic to $$\operatorname{NL}(P\to B)\otimes_BB_g \oplus(B_g\xrightarrow{g}B_g).$$

Consequently the canonical map $\operatorname{NL}_{B/A}\otimes_BB_g\to\operatorname{NL}_{B_g/A}$ is a homotopy equivalence.

Proof. The inverse-variable universal property gives $$P[X]/(I,fX-1)=B[X]/(gX-1)\cong B_g,$$ including a nilpotent $g$, when the last ring is zero. Put $q=gX-1\in B[X]$. Multiplication by $q$ is injective: if a polynomial has lowest nonzero coefficient at degree $j$, the product's coefficient at that degree is its negative. Thus the map $$B[X]/(q)\longrightarrow(q)/(q^2),\quad [a]\longmapsto[aq]$$ is an isomorphism. It is surjective by the definition of the principal ideal, and $aq=bq^2$ implies $a=bq$ by the proved multiplication injection. Therefore $(q)/(q^2)$ is free of rank one over $B_g$, with the indicated generator, also when both modules are zero.

Reduction modulo $I$ gives an exact sequence $$ (I/I^2)\otimes_BB_g\longrightarrow J/J^2 \longrightarrow(q)/(q^2)\longrightarrow0.$$ For exactness in the middle, if an element of $J$ becomes a multiple of $q^2$, lift its coefficient to $P[X]$ and subtract that coefficient times $(fX-1)^2$. The remainder lies in $IP[X]$. Its class modulo $J^2$ is a finite sum of classes of elements of $I$, with coefficients evaluated in $B_g$. This is exactly the image of the left map.

That map is injective and has a retraction. Define $$\pi:P[X]\longrightarrow(P/I^2)_f,\qquad X\longmapsto f^{-1}.$$ It maps $J$ into the square-zero ideal $I_f/I_f^2$ and maps $J^2$ to zero. The target ideal is naturally $(I/I^2)\otimes_BB_g$: the action factors through $B_g$, and localization commutes with the quotient and square by its exact fraction identities. Hence $\pi$ induces a $B_g$-linear map from $J/J^2$ to this module. On the left map its composite is the identity, proving injectivity. It kills $[fX-1]$, whose image generates the right quotient. Lifting a right-quotient coefficient by $a[fX-1]$, for $a\in B_g$, gives the asserted direct sum and proves (1).

For (2), derivations out of $P[X]$ are uniquely a derivation out of $P$ together with the chosen value of $X$. This proves the differential direct sum by the universal property, and tensoring yields the displayed formula.

Write $E=\Omega_{P/A}\otimes_PB_g$. On the first summand the conormal differential is the original $[a]\mapsto da$. On the new generator it is $$d(fX-1)=g^{-1}df+g\,dX =g\bigl(dX+g^{-2}df\bigr).$$ Changing the new differential generator from $dX$ to $w=dX+g^{-2}df$ is invertible, with inverse $dX=w-g^{-2}df$. It leaves $E$ fixed. The two direct sums now identify the entire differential with the old conormal differential plus multiplication by $g$, proving (3).

The new summand is contractible: multiplication by $g^{-1}$ from degree zero to degree one has both composites with its differential equal to the identity. Inclusion of the old summand and projection onto it therefore have composite identity there, and their other composite differs from identity by this explicit homotopy. They are homotopy inverses. The inclusion is precisely the map induced by $P\to P[X]$ and $B\to B_g$. The full presentation comparison F.11 identifies it with the stated canonical map. The argument uses neither a nonnilpotence assumption on $g$ nor a proper regular-sequence condition. ∎

Lemma F.73: product local

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 13035–13062.

If a ring $R$ has finitely many maximal ideals and locally nilpotent Jacobson radical, every prime is maximal and the natural map to the product of the corresponding localizations is an isomorphism.

Proof. Write the distinct maximal ideals as $\mathfrak m_1,\ldots,\mathfrak m_r$, and put $J=\bigcap_i\mathfrak m_i$. Each element of $J$ is nilpotent. Any prime contains $J$, hence contains $\mathfrak m_1\cdots\mathfrak m_r\subset J$. If it contained none of the factors, choosing one element outside the prime from each factor would give a product outside the prime, a contradiction. It therefore equals one of the maximal ideals.

The maximal ideals are pairwise comaximal. For two comaximal ideals $A,B$, choose $a\in A,b\in B$ with $a+b=1$; the element $ub+va$ lifts prescribed residues $u$ modulo $A$ and $v$ modulo $B$. Also $A\cap B=AB$, since $x=x(a+b)\in AB$ when $x\in A\cap B$. These identities inductively give the Chinese remainder isomorphism $$R/J\cong\prod_{i=1}^r R/\mathfrak m_i.$$ For the induction, the intersection of preceding factors is comaximal with the next one: multiply elements in the preceding maximal ideals whose residues are one modulo the next ideal. Their product lies in the intersection and still has residue one.

We give the nil-ideal idempotent lift explicitly. If $e_0^2-e_0=\epsilon$ is nilpotent, then $u=2e_0-1$ is a unit, since $u^2=1+4\epsilon$ has inverse given by a finite geometric series. Set $e_1=e_0-u^{-1}\epsilon$. Direct expansion gives $$e_1^2-e_1=u^{-2}\epsilon^2.$$ The correction lies in the nil ideal. Repeat; the error squares at each step, so a zero power of the initial error makes the process terminate at an idempotent with the prescribed residue. Uniqueness across a nil ideal follows as well: if $e,f$ are two lifts, the idempotents $e(1-f)$ and $f(1-e)$ lie in that ideal. A nilpotent idempotent is zero, so $e=ef=f$.

Lift the coordinate idempotents of $R/J$ to $e_i\in R$. Their products for distinct indices are idempotents in $J$, hence zero. Their sum is then idempotent, so $1-\sum_i e_i$ is an idempotent in $J$ and is zero. Thus $$R\longrightarrow\prod_i e_iR,\quad r\longmapsto(e_ir)_i$$ has inverse $(r_i)_i\mapsto\sum_i r_i$. Each factor, whose identity is $e_i$, has exactly one prime, corresponding to $\mathfrak m_i$, so it is local.

The factor is precisely $R_{\mathfrak m_i}$. For $s\notin\mathfrak m_i$, $e_is$ avoids its unique maximal ideal and is a unit in $e_iR$; this gives a map $R_{\mathfrak m_i}\to e_iR$. Conversely $e_i$ is an idempotent outside $\mathfrak m_i$, hence becomes one in that localization, whereas the other $e_j$ become zero. The map $e_iR\to R_{\mathfrak m_i}$ is therefore unital, and the two fraction maps are inverse. This identifies the displayed product with the natural localization map. If there are no maximal ideals, the ring is zero by the maximal-proper-ideal Zorn argument, and the empty product is the zero ring. ∎

Lemma F.74: regular quasi regular

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 17680–17766.

Let $A$ be any ring, $M$ any $A$-module, and $f_1,\ldots,f_c$ an $M$-regular sequence. Put $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$. Then the natural graded map $$ (M/JM)[T_1,\ldots,T_c]\longrightarrow \bigoplus_{n\geq0}J^nM/J^{n+1}M,\qquad \bar mT^a\longmapsto[mf^a] $$ is an isomorphism. Thus a regular sequence is quasi-regular, both for rings and for arbitrary modules. In particular, for a regular sequence in $A$, $J/J^2$ is free over $A/J$ on the classes of the $f_i$.

Proof. Every degree is generated by products of the $f_i$, so the map is surjective. Degree zero is the identity. We prove injectivity in every positive degree by induction on $c$, without finiteness or Noetherian assumptions on $M$.

For $c=1$, a relation $mf_1^n\in f_1^{n+1}M$ reads $f_1^n(m-f_1v)=0$ for some $v$. Multiplication by $f_1$ is injective on $M$, hence so is its $n$th power; thus $m\in f_1M$. For $c=0$, only degree zero is present.

Suppose now $c>1$ and the assertion holds for the first $c-1$ entries; write $J'=(f_1,\ldots,f_{c-1})$ and $f'= (f_1,\ldots,f_{c-1})$. A degree-$n$ relation modulo $J^{n+1}M$ can be made an exact zero relation by subtracting, from each coefficient, an element of $JM$: every element of $J^{n+1}M$ is a sum of degree-$n$ products with coefficients in $JM$. It suffices therefore to handle $$\sum_{e=0}^{\ell}\ \sum_{|a|=n-e}m_{a,e}(f')^a f_c^e=0 \quad(0\leq\ell\leq n).$$ Induct on its largest exponent $\ell$. If $\ell=0$, the induction on $c$ applied in degree $n$ gives all coefficients in $J'M\subset JM$. For $\ell\geq1$, every lower-exponent term belongs to $J'^{\,n-\ell+1}M$. Consequently $$\sum_{|a|=n-\ell}(f_c^\ell m_{a,\ell})(f')^a \in J'^{\,n-\ell+1}M.$$ The already proved degree-$n-\ell$ assertion for the shorter list gives $f_c^\ell m_{a,\ell}\in J'M$; in degree zero this is simply membership in $J'M$. Since $f_c$ is injective on $M/J'M$, its powers are injective there, and hence $m_{a,\ell}\in J'M$.

Write each such coefficient as $\sum_{j<c}f_jb_{a,j}$. Replace its top term by $$m_{a,\ell}(f')^af_c^\ell =\sum_{j<c}(f_cb_{a,j})(f')^{a+\delta_j}f_c^{\ell-1}.$$ The new relation has largest exponent at most $\ell-1$, and the only changed coefficients differ from the old ones by elements of $f_cM\subset JM$. The induction on $\ell$ puts all new coefficients in $JM$. It therefore puts all old lower coefficients in $JM$, and the old top coefficients were already in $J'M$. This proves the homogeneous injectivity for every $n$ and completes both inductions.

Taking $M=A$ proves the ring assertion. Its degree-one isomorphism is exactly $(A/J)^c\to J/J^2$, with the stated basis. No permutation of the regular list, separatedness, or finite-module hypothesis has been used. ∎

Lemma F.75: regular sequence in polynomial ring

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 17576–17624.

Let $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in R$ generate a proper ideal in an arbitrary ring. These conditions are equivalent:

  1. Every permutation of the list is regular.
  2. Every subsequence in its original order is regular.
  3. $f_1X_1,\ldots,f_rX_r$ is regular in $R[X_1,\ldots,X_r]$.

Proof. A subsequence can be placed first in a permutation, so (1) implies (2). To prove the converse we first check the interchange of two elements. If $a,b$ is regular and $b$ is also a nonzerodivisor, then $b,a$ is regular. Indeed, if $ax=by$, injectivity of $b$ modulo $(a)$ gives $y=az$. Injectivity of $a$ then gives $x=bz$, proving injectivity of $a$ modulo $(b)$. The final ideal is the same proper ideal.

Induct on $r$ to deduce (1) from (2). Any proper sublist inherits (2), so by induction all its permutations are regular. Given a permutation whose last entry is $f_s$, the preceding entries are therefore regular, and it remains to check that $f_s$ is injective modulo all the others. If $s=r$, this is the last injection of the original list. If $s<r$, put $$V=R/(f_1,\ldots,\widehat f_s,\ldots,f_{r-1}).$$ Permuting the first $r-1$ entries shows that $f_s$ is a nonzerodivisor on $V$. The original-order subsequence omitting $f_s$ shows that $f_r$ is one too. The pair $f_s,f_r$ is regular in $V$, since its second injection is the final injection of the original full list. The two-element interchange just proved makes $f_r,f_s$ regular in $V$, giving the required last injection. All quotient ideals are proper because they are contained in the original proper ideal.

For the polynomial condition, the coefficient of each monomial is independent of the coefficients of the others. After imposing the first $i$ equations, this gives the exact $R$-module decomposition $$ R[X]/(f_1X_1,\ldots,f_iX_i) \cong\bigoplus_{e\in\mathbf N^r}(R/J_e)\,X^e,\qquad J_e=(f_j\mid j\leq i,\ e_j>0). $$ To verify it, a multiple of $f_jX_j$ contributes to the coefficient of $X^e$ precisely when $e_j>0$, and then contributes a multiple of $f_j$. Conversely any such coefficient is obtained by multiplying $f_jX_j$ by that monomial with its $j$th exponent reduced by one. These two calculations identify the entire ideal coefficient by coefficient.

Multiplication by $f_{i+1}X_{i+1}$ shifts each exponent to $e+\delta_{i+1}$ and multiplies its coefficient by $f_{i+1}$. The coefficient ideal $J_e$ is unchanged by this shift, since only the first $i$ indices occur in it. The multiplication is injective precisely when $f_{i+1}$ is injective on every $R/J_e$.

Under (2), the ordered list with indices $\{j\leq i:e_j>0\}$ followed by $i+1$ is a regular subsequence, giving every such injection. This proves (3). Conversely, for any subset $U\subset\{1,\ldots,i\}$ choose $e_j=1$ for $j\in U$ and zero otherwise. The injection supplied by (3) says that $f_{i+1}$ is injective on $R/(f_j:j\in U)$. Apply it successively along any ordered subsequence to prove all of (2). The polynomial equation ideal is proper since evaluation at all $X_j=0$ factors its quotient onto the nonzero ring $R$. For the empty list all three conditions hold directly. ∎

Lemma F.76: relative global complete intersection

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38280–38292.

A relative global complete intersection over any commutative base ring is syntomic.

Proof. Write its presentation as $S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$, with every nonempty residue-field fibre of dimension $n-c$, as in the relative complete-intersection definition. The finite generator and equation lists give finite presentation. The entire arbitrary-base proof F.77 gives flatness of $S$ over $R$.

Each nonempty fibre has the displayed $n$ polynomial variables, $c$ equations and dimension $n-c$, so is a global complete intersection over its field. It is consequently locally a complete intersection: the whole five-condition proof F.57 applies at every fibre prime, or its global presentation itself is the required neighbourhood. Empty fibres have no point to check. These are the finite-presentation, flatness and fibre conditions for syntomicness. If $S=0$, finite presentation is $R/(1)$, flatness is immediate, and all fibres are empty, giving the same conclusion. ∎

Lemma F.77: relative global complete intersection conormal

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38204–38278.

Let $R$ be any ring and $$S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$$ a relative global complete intersection: every nonempty residue-field fibre has dimension $n-c$. For a prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$, let $\mathfrak Q\subset R[X]$ be its inverse image. Then:

  1. $f_1,\ldots,f_c$ is regular in $R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}$.
  2. Every $R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)$, including $i=0$, is flat over $R$.
  3. The global $S$-module $(f)/(f)^2$ is free on the classes of the $f_i$.

In particular $S$ is flat over $R$. These assertions include bases that are not Noetherian.

Proof. First take a Noetherian base. Fix $\mathfrak Q$ and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak Q\cap R$, $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. Its closed polynomial fibre is a localization of $k[X]$ at the corresponding prime. In the nonempty quotient fibre, every minimal equation prime has height at most $c$, by the whole AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.1. The polynomial height formula AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3, makes each component dimension at least $n-c$. Their maximum is the assumed dimension $n-c$, so all have this dimension. The point formula of AG-CA-09, Theorem 6.1, gives dimension $n-c$ at the chosen quotient point. Thus F.20 gives local dimension drop exactly $c$ for this polynomial presentation. The full criterion F.57 makes its actual $c$-element equation list regular in the ambient fibre local ring.

The map $R_{\mathfrak p}\to R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}$ is flat and local: a polynomial ring is free, and localization preserves exact tensor injection tests. Both rings are Noetherian. Apply the complete successive-quotient lifting proof F.53. It proves both regularity in the polynomial local ring and flatness of every local successive quotient over $R_{\mathfrak p}$, hence over $R$.

For the general base we construct a finite Noetherian coefficient model. We first justify the field-dimension fact needed in this descent. For a nonzero finite-type $k$-algebra $C$, the entire AG-CA-09, Corollary 3.2 gives an inclusion $k[T_1,\ldots,T_d]\subset C$ with $C$ finite over it, even when $C$ is not reduced or a domain. For any field extension $E/k$, a basis makes its tensor functor free and faithfully flat. Thus the inclusion remains an inclusion of $E[T]$ into $C\otimes_kE$, and finiteness remains true. The entire AG-CA-05, Theorem 5.1 and polynomial dimension AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.2, give $$\dim C=d=\dim(C\otimes_kE).$$ The zero algebra stays zero. This proves precisely the field-extension dimension preservation used below.

Let $R_a\subset R$ be generated over the image of $\mathbf Z$ by all coefficients of the equations, and put $S_a=R_a[X]/(f)$. These are finite-type Noetherian models, and $S=R\otimes_{R_a}S_a$. At any actual $\mathfrak q\subset S$, let $\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q_a,\mathfrak p_a$ be its contractions. The residue fields give an inclusion $\kappa(\mathfrak p_a)\subset\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, and the two corresponding fibres are related by that scalar tensor. The latter is nonempty, since the prime $\mathfrak q$ lies over $\mathfrak p$. Its dimension is $n-c$. The proved field-dimension fact therefore gives that dimension for the model fibre as well.

The whole arbitrary-base neighbourhood proof F.39 supplies $g_{\mathfrak q}\in S_a\setminus\mathfrak q_a$ whose localized model fibres all have dimension at most $n-c$. Indeed its bound is the dimension at the chosen fibre point, which is at most its total dimension $n-c$; a bound at every point bounds the total dimension by testing the finitely many component generic points. The resulting opens pull back to a cover of $\operatorname{Spec}S$. Choose finitely many, defined by $g_1,\ldots,g_m$, by affine quasi-compactness: their images generate the unit ideal, because otherwise a maximal ideal would give an uncovered point.

Choose polynomial representatives $G_j\in R_a[X]$. A unit-ideal relation in $S$ has a finite polynomial witness $$1=\sum_j H_jG_j+\sum_i V_if_i\quad\text{in }R[X].$$ Adjoin to $R_a$ all coefficients of the finitely many $H_j,V_i$, obtaining a finite-type integer subalgebra $R_0\subset R$. Set $S_0=R_0[X]/(f)$. The same identity now holds in $R_0[X]$, so the images of the $G_j$ cover $\operatorname{Spec}S_0$.

For every base prime of $R_0$, its residue field extends that of its contraction in $R_a$. Each chart fibre is therefore the corresponding old chart fibre after a field extension. It retains dimension at most $n-c$ by the proved dimension fact. A finite open cover has total dimension the maximum of the chart dimensions here: in a finite-type field algebra each component's generic point belongs to some chart, and that nonempty principal component open retains its dimension. Thus every nonempty fibre of $S_0/R_0$ has dimension at most $n-c$. The height bound for an ideal generated by $c$ elements in a polynomial ring gives the reverse inequality at any minimal equation prime. Every nonempty model fibre consequently has dimension exactly $n-c$. This constructs the required Noetherian relative global complete-intersection model, with the identical equation list and $$S=R\otimes_{R_0}S_0.$$ If $S=0$, a finite identity $1=\sum_iV_if_i$ already gives a model with $S_0=0$. The local claims are then vacuous and both conormal modules are zero; hence we may continue with a chosen actual prime.

Contract $\mathfrak Q$ to $\mathfrak Q_0\subset R_0[X]$ and $\mathfrak p_0\subset R_0$. Put $$A_0=(R_0)_{\mathfrak p_0},\qquad B_0=(R_0[X])_{\mathfrak Q_0},\qquad B_i=B_0/(f_1,\ldots,f_i).$$ The Noetherian case gives regularity and $A_0$-flatness of each $B_i$, so for every $i<c$ there is an exact sequence $$0\longrightarrow B_i\xrightarrow{f_{i+1}}B_i \longrightarrow B_{i+1}\longrightarrow0.$$ Tensor it with $R_{\mathfrak p}$ over $A_0$. It remains left exact because its quotient $B_{i+1}$ is $A_0$-flat: the full Tor long exact sequence AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A gives zero for the possible first kernel. This is the exact reason regularity survives this possibly nonflat scalar change. Base change also makes each $B_i\otimes_{A_0}R_{\mathfrak p}$ flat over $R_{\mathfrak p}$, by the tensor associativity formula for injection tests.

The further prime localization of $B_0\otimes_{A_0}R_{\mathfrak p}$ at the prime induced by $\mathfrak Q$ is exactly $R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}$. To check this, the tensor first inverts the images of $R_0[X]\setminus\mathfrak Q_0$, all of which avoid the actual prime. The further localization inverts the remaining polynomials outside $\mathfrak Q$. Every fraction in the full prime localization is then represented, and the two localization universal properties give inverse maps. Taking the same localizations of the quotient tensors gives exactly $R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)$. Exact localization preserves each displayed multiplication injection and its quotient. Its last quotient is $S_{\mathfrak q}\ne0$, so the resulting list is regular. Localization preserves flatness of these target modules, and $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is flat over $R$. This proves (1) and (2) over the original arbitrary base.

Finally F.74 gives the conormal basis at every prime of $S$. The global map $S^c\to(f)/(f)^2$ is surjective by generation. Localization commutes with this ideal quotient; its kernel vanishes at every prime by the local bases. A nonzero module element would have a proper annihilator contained in a maximal ideal and would stay nonzero there, so the kernel is zero. This proves (3). For any injection of $R$-modules the tensor kernel with $S$ likewise vanishes after localization at every $\mathfrak q$, by (2) for its final quotient. The same module detection proves that kernel zero. Thus $S$ is flat over $R$, as asserted. Empty equation lists are included at every step. ∎

Lemma F.78: relative global complete intersection smooth

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 39071–39113.

For a relative global complete-intersection presentation $S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ over any ring $R$, smoothness at a prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ is equivalent to some $c\times c$ Jacobian minor having image outside $\mathfrak q$.
