In the polynomial differential basis the conormal map is $$J:S^c\longrightarrow S^n,\qquad e_j\longmapsto\sum_i\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial X_i}\,dX_i.$$ Thus its maximal minors are precisely the stated polynomials.

If a selected minor $\Delta$ has image $g\notin\mathfrak q$, then $S_g$ has the inverse-variable presentation $$S_g=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n,Z]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,\Delta Z-1).$$ Use the selected $c$ variable columns together with $Z$. Its square Jacobian block has the original selected block at the top, a zero top-right column, and $\Delta$ at the bottom right. Its determinant is $\Delta^2$, a unit in this algebra. The entire arbitrary-base standard smooth lifting proof AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1 therefore makes this finitely presented algebra smooth. This proves the sufficient direction with an actual principal neighbourhood.

Conversely suppose some $S_h$, with $h\notin\mathfrak q$, is smooth. Its polynomial inverse-variable presentation has a split conormal map by the complete split-sequence proof AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1. The entire F.72 calculation identifies its conormal complex with the original localized complex $$S_h^c\xrightarrow{J_h}S_h^n$$ plus a contractible rank-one complex, whose differential is multiplication by the unit $h$. In these explicitly changed bases, restrict a left inverse of the full differential to the original degree-zero summand, and project its values to the original degree-one summand. The composite is a left inverse of $J_h$. Reduction to $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ preserves this identity. Hence the resulting $n$-by-$c$ matrix has rank $c$, and the full minor calculation F.70 supplies a nonzero $c$-minor over that field. Its original image is outside $\mathfrak q$, proving necessity.

For $c=0$ the empty minor is one and the presentation is a polynomial algebra, smooth by arbitrary variable lifting. Thus this case obeys the same criterion. No Noetherian condition on the base or the target is used. ∎

Lemma F.79: section smooth

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 39859–39914.

Let $R\to S$ be smooth and let $\sigma:S\to R$ be its section, with $I=\ker\sigma$. Then $I/I^2$ is finite projective over $R$. If it is free of rank $d$, the $I$-adic completion of $S$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to $R[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]]$.

Proof. Define $$D:S\longrightarrow I/I^2,\qquad D(s)=[s-\sigma(s)].$$ Give the target its $S$-module action through $\sigma$. Expanding a product and discarding the product of two elements of $I$ proves the derivation identity. It is an $R$-derivation. The universal differential map therefore induces $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_{S,\sigma}R\to I/I^2$. Its inverse sends $[i]$ to $di\otimes1$. This is well-defined since $d(ij)$ vanishes after tensoring for $i,j\in I$; on every $ds$ its composite is $d(s-\sigma(s))=ds$, and on every ideal class its other composite is the identity. Thus the two maps are inverse.

The entire AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1 gives finite projectivity of the differential module of this finitely presented formally smooth algebra. Tensor of its finite free direct-summand description with $R$ retains that description, proving the first assertion. The section ideal is finite as well: if $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ are finite algebra generators, the polynomial difference identity makes the $x_j-\sigma(x_j)$ generate its kernel.

Choose $t_1,\ldots,t_d\in I$ representing a free conormal basis, and put $P=R[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]]$, $J=(T_1,\ldots,T_d)$. Continuous evaluation defines $$b:P\longrightarrow\widehat S=\varprojlim_n S/I^n,\qquad T_i\longmapsto t_i.$$ This map is surjective. To see it, every element of $I$ is an $R$-linear combination of the $t_i$ modulo $I^2$. Multiplying these expressions shows that the degree-$n$ monomials in the $t_i$ generate $I^n/I^{n+1}$ over $R$ for every $n$. Start with the constant residue of a chosen element of $\widehat S$, which is in $S/I=R$. At step $n$, the error in its coordinate modulo $I^{n+1}$ lies in $I^n/I^{n+1}$, so subtract a homogeneous degree-$n$ polynomial in the $t_i$ with coefficients in $R$. The resulting sum of homogeneous corrections is a formal series in $P$, with image the chosen compatible sequence. This proves surjectivity without a Noetherian completion theorem.

The square-zero section decomposition $S/I^2=R\oplus I/I^2$ defines an $R$-map $u_2:S\to P/J^2$, sending the chosen $t_i$ to $T_i$. Formal smoothness lifts it successively along $$P/J^{n+1}\longrightarrow P/J^n\quad(n\geq2),$$ whose kernel $J^n/J^{n+1}$ has square zero. Choose each lift to extend the preceding one. Their inverse limit is an $R$-map $u:S\to P$ taking $I$ into $J$. Therefore the maps modulo $J^n$ factor through $S/I^n$ and give a continuous extension $a:\widehat S\to P$.

The composite $v=ab$ is an $R$-endomorphism of $P$ with $$v(T_i)=T_i+\text{terms of degree at least two}.$$ We prove that such a substitution is invertible. Having chosen inverse variable series through degree $n-1$, compute the degree-$n$ error after substitution. Adding its negative as the next homogeneous term removes it, since the identity linear part changes that degree by exactly the added term; all nonlinear changes have higher degree. This recursively constructs a right inverse. The substitution is injective: any nonzero series has a lowest nonzero homogeneous part, and the identity linear part leaves that part unchanged. If $w$ is the right inverse, then $v(wv)=v$; injectivity gives $wv=1$, proving that it is also a left inverse. The coefficient calculations hold over arbitrary $R$, including zero divisors.

Replace $a$ by $v^{-1}a$. Now $ab=1$; hence $b$ is injective, and it was already proved surjective. It is the desired $R$-algebra isomorphism. All maps are continuous for the displayed adic topologies. When $d=0$, the homogeneous correction argument gives $\widehat S=R$ directly, and the same assertion holds. ∎

Lemma F.80: silly

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 00DS.

Let \(J,I_1,\ldots,I_r\) be ideals of any commutative ring. Suppose \(J\not\subset I_i\) for every \(i\), and at most two of the \(I_i\) are not prime. There is an element of \(J\) outside all the \(I_i\).

Proof. Remove repetitions and every listed ideal contained in another listed ideal. Avoiding the retained larger ideals also avoids the removed smaller ones. The remaining ideals are pairwise incomparable, and still at most two are not prime. We prove the assertion for this remaining list by induction on its length.

For the empty list choose \(0\in J\); there are no avoidance conditions. For one ideal the hypothesis supplies an element outside it. For two ideals choose \(a\in J\setminus I_1\) and \(b\in J\setminus I_2\). If either avoids both, it suffices. Otherwise \(a\in I_2\), \(b\in I_1\). Their sum belongs to neither: membership in \(I_1\) would force \(a=(a+b)-b\in I_1\), and membership in \(I_2\) would similarly force \(b\in I_2\).

For a list of length at least three, place a prime ideal last, calling it \(\mathfrak p=I_r\). Induction gives \(a\in J\) outside all earlier ideals. If \(a\notin\mathfrak p\), it already suffices. Otherwise choose \(b_0\in J\setminus\mathfrak p\) and, for each \(i<r\), choose \(b_i\in I_i\setminus\mathfrak p\); incomparability supplies the latter choices. The product \(b=b_0b_1\cdots b_{r-1}\) belongs to \(J\) and every earlier \(I_i\). It lies outside \(\mathfrak p\), because iterating the defining implication for a prime ideal shows that a product of elements outside it stays outside. Then \(a+b\in J\) still avoids every earlier ideal by subtraction of \(b\), and avoids \(\mathfrak p\) by subtraction of \(a\). This completes the induction without a Noetherian hypothesis. ∎

Lemma F.81: size extension pth roots

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 45787–45812.

Let $k$ have characteristic $p>0$. If $da_1,\ldots,da_n$ are linearly independent in $\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}$, then $$[k(a_1^{1/p},\ldots,a_n^{1/p}):k]=p^n.$$

Proof. Roots can be adjoined successively by quotienting by an irreducible factor of $X^p-a_i$. Such a factor exists by descent on degree, and its quotient is a field by the Euclidean algorithm. A $p$th root is unique in any field containing it: equal $p$th powers give $(x-y)^p=0$, hence $x=y$. Thus these compatible adjunctions give the asserted root field.

We also prove the degree at a nontrivial step. If $\beta^p=a\in H$ and $\beta\notin H$, its minimal polynomial divides $X^p-a=(X-\beta)^p$ in a field containing $\beta$. A monic proper nonconstant factor has degree $r$ with $1\leq r<p$ and coefficient $-r\beta$ at degree $r-1$. If it were over $H$, the nonzero scalar $r$ would put $\beta$ in $H$, a contradiction. Thus the minimal polynomial has degree $p$, and monic division gives the basis $1,\beta,\ldots,\beta^{p-1}$.

Induct on the number of roots already adjoined. The zero-root extension is $k$, of degree one. Suppose the first $i-1$ roots have degree $p^{i-1}$ and the standard monomials in them form a $k$-basis. If $a_i$ were a $p$th power in that field, a root could be written in that basis. Raising it to the $p$th power would give $$a_i=\sum_{0\leq e_j<p}\lambda_e^p\prod_{j<i}a_j^{e_j}, \qquad \lambda_e\in k.$$ Every $p$th power in $k$ has zero differential, directly from the derivation product rule. Differentiating this finite equality therefore gives $$ da_i=\sum_e\ \sum_{\substack{j<i\\e_j>0}} e_j\lambda_e^p\,a_j^{e_j-1} \left(\prod_{\substack{\ell<i\\\ell\ne j}}a_\ell^{e_\ell}\right)da_j. $$ This is a linear dependence on the earlier differentials, contrary to the hypothesis. For $i=1$ the right side is empty, giving the same contradiction. Hence the next root is not in the preceding field; the degree-$p$ calculation applies. Its power basis multiplied by the old monomial basis gives the new monomial basis, proving both independence and generation. Degrees multiply along these finite vector-space towers, so the final degree is $p^n$. This also covers $n=0$, and uses no converse criterion for zero absolute differentials. ∎

Lemma F.82: smooth over field

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38622–38676.

Every smooth finite-type algebra over any field is locally a complete intersection.

Proof. Let $S/k$ be smooth and choose a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$. The full principal-chart proof AG-CA-17, Theorem 5.1 supplies a standard smooth neighbourhood $D=S_h$ containing it. Write its polynomial presentation as $$D=k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_N]/(F_1,\ldots,F_r),$$ with an invertible $r$-column Jacobian minor. Let $\mathfrak Q$ be the polynomial prime over the chosen point and put $V=k[Y]_{\mathfrak Q}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak QV$.

The classes of the $F_i$ in $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ are independent. Indeed the differential of a product of two elements of $\mathfrak m$ is zero after tensoring with its residue field. A relation among these classes would consequently give the same residue-field relation among the vectors $dF_i$; derivatives of its lifted coefficients multiply $F_i$ and vanish in that residue field. The chosen nonzero Jacobian minor makes these vectors independent, proving the assertion. This does not assume that the entire cotangent-to-differential map is injective.

The entire polynomial-local regularity proof AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3 makes $V$ regular. Extend the independent classes to a basis of its finite-dimensional cotangent space and lift the added classes to $\mathfrak m$. Nakayama makes this list a minimal generating list for $\mathfrak m$. The whole AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1 proves that every such list is regular in this order. Its initial list $F_1,\ldots,F_r$ is therefore regular and generates the defining ideal in $V$.

Condition (5) of the entire criterion F.57 now gives a principal global complete-intersection neighbourhood of this point in $D$. Its denominator is some $a/h^e$ with $a\in S$, so the same neighbourhood in $\operatorname{Spec}S$ is $D(ha)$, with the identical iterated localization as coordinate algebra. Every point thus has a global complete-intersection principal neighbourhood. This is precisely local complete-intersectionness over $k$. The argument treats arbitrary primes and fields, including imperfect fields. For $S=0$ its empty spectrum already has the required empty cover. ∎

Lemma F.83: smooth syntomic

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 00TA.

A smooth map $R\to S$ admits a cover of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ by principal opens $D(g)$ for which $S_g$ is standard smooth over $R$. When $R$ is Noetherian, the map is also syntomic.

Proof. The case $S=0$ has an empty cover. The zero algebra has the finite presentation $R/(1)$, is flat as a zero module, and has no nonempty fibres, so it also satisfies the asserted syntomic condition. Hence consider a nonzero $S$.

Fix a finite presentation $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\twoheadrightarrow S$ with kernel $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$, and put $M=I/I^2$. The split conormal theorem AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1 puts $M$ inside $S^n$ as a direct summand. Its complement is finite, because projections of the coordinate vectors generate it. The splitting therefore presents $M$ finitely; it also proves flatness by restricting tensor injections for the free module. S01, Lemma 1.2 makes $M$ free over each local ring.

For a subset $E$ of the equation indices, let $U_E$ be the points where the classes indexed by $E$ are a basis of $M$. These loci are open and cover the spectrum. Here are the denominator details. At a prime $\mathfrak q$, select a basis of the residue vector space from the spanning equation classes, with $r$ selected members. Their map $\varphi:S^r\to M$ is surjective over $S_{\mathfrak q}$ by Nakayama. In a local free basis its matrix is square and invertible modulo the maximal ideal, hence invertible by the determinant and adjugate identities. The finite cokernel vanishes at $\mathfrak q$; multiplying denominators which kill its generators gives $a\notin\mathfrak q$ with $\varphi_a$ surjective. Since $M_a$ is projective, its kernel is a finite summand of $S_a^r$. It vanishes at $\mathfrak q$ too. Multiplying numerators of denominators which kill its generators gives $b\notin\mathfrak q$ with $\varphi_{ab}$ an isomorphism. Thus $D(ab)$ lies in this basis locus. The same reasoning applies at every point of any fixed $U_E$, proving openness. Selecting a basis from a spanning vector-space list proves covering. For rank zero the selected list is empty and empty denominator products are $1$.

Choose principal opens inside these loci. On one such open $D(g)$, adjoining a variable representing $g^{-1}$ gives a finite polynomial presentation whose conormal module, by F.72, is $M_g\oplus S_g$. It is free. F.55 then supplies a polynomial presentation of $S_g$ whose kernel is generated by a list which is itself a conormal basis. Denote this algebra temporarily by $T$, and write its presentation as $$ R[y_1,\ldots,y_N]\twoheadrightarrow T, \qquad K=(a_1,\ldots,a_c),\qquad K/K^2=T^c. $$

The conormal differential has a left inverse. In these bases let its matrix be $A:T^c\to T^N$, and let $B:T^N\to T^c$ satisfy $BA=1$. At a residue field this forces $c\le N$. The determinant expansion F.70(2) shows that its $c$-row minors $\Delta_E$ generate $1$. Each selected square map is invertible precisely on $D(\Delta_E)$, by the adjugate formula, so these principal opens cover $\operatorname{Spec}T$. The empty minor for $c=0$ is $1$.

On a selected minor open, order its $c$ pivot variables first and let $h\in R[y]$ represent the inverted element $u=\Delta_E\in T$. Present $T_u$ by $a_1,\ldots,a_c,hz-1$. Its Jacobian on $y_1,\ldots,y_c,z$ has diagonal blocks the selected Jacobian and $u$, and upper right block zero. Its determinant is $u\Delta_E$, a unit. This is a standard smooth presentation. Finally a principal open in $S_g$ is principal in $S$: write its defining fraction as $s/g^k$, so its open corresponds to $D(gs)$. The charts just constructed are consequently the required principal cover of the original spectrum.

If $R$ is Noetherian, F.85 makes each chart a relative global complete intersection. F.76 makes it syntomic, and F.62 glues that condition on the target. This proves the last assertion. ∎

Lemma F.84: snake

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07JW.

Suppose the following diagram of abelian groups commutes and both rows are exact: $$ \begin{array}{ccccccccc} &&X&\xrightarrow{a}&Y&\xrightarrow{b}&Z&\longrightarrow&0\\ &&\alpha\downarrow&&\beta\downarrow&&\gamma\downarrow\\ 0&\longrightarrow&U&\xrightarrow{i}&V&\xrightarrow{j}&W. \end{array} $$ There is a canonical exact sequence $$ \ker\alpha\xrightarrow{a}\ker\beta\xrightarrow{b}\ker\gamma \xrightarrow{\partial}\operatorname{coker}\alpha \xrightarrow{i}\operatorname{coker}\beta \xrightarrow{j}\operatorname{coker}\gamma. $$ Its first map is injective if $a$ is injective, and its last map is surjective if $j$ is surjective.

Proof. For $z\in\ker\gamma$, choose $y$ with $b(y)=z$. Commutativity gives $j\beta(y)=0$, so exactness supplies $u$ with $i(u)=\beta(y)$. The injection $i$ makes this $u$ unique for the chosen $y$. Define $\partial z=[u]$ modulo $\alpha(X)$. Replacing $y$ by another lift changes it by $a(x)$; commutativity and injectivity of $i$ then change $u$ by $\alpha(x)$. Thus the class is independent of the lift. Adding lifts proves additivity. The other arrows are the restrictions or quotient maps induced by $a,b,i,j$, which are well defined by the commutative squares.

For exactness at $\ker\beta$, take $y$ there with $b(y)=0$. Write $y=a(x)$. Since $i\alpha(x)=\beta a(x)=0$ and $i$ is injective, $x\in\ker\alpha$. Conversely the image of such an $x$ lies in that kernel and has zero $b$-image.

At $\ker\gamma$, the condition $\partial z=0$ says that the chosen $u$ is $\alpha(x)$ for some $x$. Subtract $a(x)$ from the chosen $y$. This still maps to $z$, and its $\beta$-image is zero. Conversely a lift already in $\ker\beta$ allows $u=0$, so has zero connecting class.

At $\operatorname{coker}\alpha$, a class $[u]$ dies in $\operatorname{coker}\beta$ exactly when $i(u)=\beta(y)$ for some $y$. Then $z=b(y)$ satisfies $\gamma(z)=j\beta(y)=ji(u)=0$, and the defining lift gives $\partial z=[u]$. Every connecting class has zero image for this same reason.

At $\operatorname{coker}\beta$, a class $[v]$ dies in $\operatorname{coker}\gamma$ exactly when $j(v)=\gamma(z)$ for some $z$. Lift $z$ to $y\in Y$. The element $v-\beta(y)$ has zero $j$-image, so is $i(u)$ by bottom-row exactness. Hence $[v]$ comes from $[u]$. Conversely $ji=0$ kills every such image. These checks prove exactness at every intermediate term. Restriction of an injective $a$ remains injective. If $j$ is onto, lift any representative in $W$ to $V$ to obtain surjectivity on the last cokernel. ∎

Lemma F.85: standard smooth

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 00T7.

Let $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$, and $S=P/I$ be standard smooth, with the first $c$ variables chosen as pivots. Then:

  1. $R\to S$ is smooth.
  2. $\Omega_{S/R}$ has the free basis $dx_{c+1},\ldots,dx_n$.
  3. $I/I^2$ has the free basis $[f_1],\ldots,[f_c]$.
  4. Every principal localization $S_g$ is standard smooth over $R$.
  5. For every base map $R\to R'$, the algebra $R'\otimes_R S$ is standard smooth over $R'$.
  6. If $r\in R$ becomes a unit in $S$, then $S$ is standard smooth over $R_r$.
  7. This presentation makes $S$ a relative global complete intersection over $R$.

Proof. Let $C=(\partial f_i/\partial x_j)_{1\le i,j\le c}$; its determinant is a unit in $S$. The map $S^c\to I/I^2$ taking the standard vectors to the equation classes is onto. Its composite with the conormal differential and projection onto the first $c$ differential coordinates is an invertible matrix (the transpose of $C$ under column-vector conventions). Thus this surjection is injective as well. The equation classes are a basis, and the conormal differential is split injective.

Write its image in $S^n$ as the columns of $\binom{C^{\mathsf t}}{D}$. An arbitrary vector $(v,w)$ differs from a unique conormal vector by $$ (v,w)-\binom{C^{\mathsf t}}{D}(C^{\mathsf t})^{-1}v =(0,w-D(C^{\mathsf t})^{-1}v). $$ The conormal image meets the last coordinate summand only in zero. Its cokernel is therefore exactly that summand, with the asserted differential basis. Finite presentation and this split conormal sequence give smoothness by the complete criterion AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1 and Section 4. This proves (1)–(3), including $c=0$.

To invert $g$, choose a polynomial $h$ representing it and use the equations $f_1,\ldots,f_c,hz-1$. On pivot variables $x_1,\ldots,x_c,z$, the Jacobian has blocks $$ \begin{pmatrix}C&0\\z(\partial h/\partial x_1,\ldots,\partial h/\partial x_c)&h\end{pmatrix}. $$ Its determinant $h\det C$ is a unit in $S_g$. This proves (4), even when the localization is zero. Under a base map, applying the map to every coefficient presents the tensor product; the same operation takes the determinant to its image, which remains invertible. This proves (5). For (6), the original equations over $R_r$ present $S_r=S$, since the image of $r$ is already invertible; their determinant is unchanged.

For (7), it remains to compute every nonempty fibre's dimension. By (5) such a fibre is a nonzero standard smooth algebra $B=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(\bar f_1,\ldots,\bar f_c)$ over its residue field $k$. It is locally a complete intersection by F.82. At any prime $\mathfrak q$ of $B$, let $\mathfrak q'$ be its polynomial preimage. The conormal module is free of rank $c$ by (3); reducing to the residue field determines that rank uniquely. F.57 identifies it with $\operatorname{height}(\mathfrak q')-\operatorname{height}(\mathfrak q)$. For a minimal prime $\mathfrak q$ this gives $\operatorname{height}(\mathfrak q')=c$. The polynomial height formula AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3 therefore gives dimension $n-c$ for every component.

The algebra $B$ is Noetherian by S01, Lemma 1.3, so F.136 and F.137 give a finite component cover. Dimension equals the largest component dimension: a finite chain of irreducible closed subsets lies in a component containing its largest member, and every chain inside a component is also a chain in the whole space. Thus $\dim B=n-c$. This argument works over imperfect fields and for an empty equation list. Empty fibres require no dimension assertion, completing (7). ∎

Lemma F.86: sum two terms

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 00S3.

Let $A_1\xrightarrow{d_A}A_0$ and $B_1\xrightarrow{d_B}B_0$ be two-term complexes of modules over a ring. If they are homotopy equivalent, then $$ A_1\oplus B_0\cong B_1\oplus A_0. $$

Proof. Choose chain maps $\varphi:A_\bullet\to B_\bullet$ and $\psi:B_\bullet\to A_\bullet$ and homotopies $h:A_0\to A_1$, $h':B_0\to B_1$ with $$ 1-\psi_1\varphi_1=hd_A,\qquad 1-\psi_0\varphi_0=d_Ah, $$ $$ 1-\varphi_1\psi_1=h'd_B,\qquad 1-\varphi_0\psi_0=d_Bh'. $$ Define $U:B_1\oplus A_0\to A_1\oplus B_0$ and $V$ in the reverse direction by $$ U=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_1&h\\-d_B&\varphi_0\end{pmatrix},\qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}\varphi_1&-h'\\d_A&\psi_0\end{pmatrix}. $$ Multiplying the blocks and using the four homotopy identities and the two chain-map identities gives $$ UV=\begin{pmatrix}1&h\psi_0-\psi_1h'\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad VU=\begin{pmatrix}1&\varphi_1h-h'\varphi_0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}. $$ Each off-diagonal matrix squares to zero, so negating that off-diagonal block gives the inverse product. Consequently $L=(VU)^{-1}V$ is a left inverse of $U$, and $T=V(UV)^{-1}$ is a right inverse. The equality $L=L(UT)=(LU)T=T$ makes them the same inverse. Hence $U$ is an isomorphism, proving the claim without any finite-generation or freeness hypothesis. ∎

Lemma F.87: syntomic

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 00SY.

Let $R$ be Noetherian, and let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ lie over $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$. The following neighbourhood conditions are equivalent:

  1. Some $g\notin\mathfrak q$ makes $R\to S_g$ syntomic.
  2. Some $g\notin\mathfrak q$ makes $S_g$ a relative global complete intersection over $R$.
  3. Some $g\notin\mathfrak q$ makes $S_g$ finitely presented over $R$, while $R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat and $S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}$ is a complete-intersection local ring over $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ in the sense of F.3.

Proof. A syntomic neighbourhood is finitely presented and flat and has locally complete-intersection fibres; F.58 gives (3) from (1). F.76 gives (1) from (2). We prove the remaining implication with all rings localized explicitly.

Under (3), first replace $S$ by the indicated finitely presented neighbourhood, retaining the prime. Write $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\twoheadrightarrow S$ with kernel $I$ and polynomial preimage $\mathfrak q'$. In the fibre $\bar P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, write $\bar I$ for the image ideal and $\bar{\mathfrak q}'$ for the induced prime. By F.58 and F.57, the ideal $\bar I_{\bar{\mathfrak q}'}$ has a regular generating list of length $c$, its minimal number of generators. Choose $f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I$ whose images give a basis of $\bar I_{\bar{\mathfrak q}'}/\bar{\mathfrak q}'\bar I_{\bar{\mathfrak q}'}$. This is possible by selecting a basis from the images of a finite generating list of $I$. Nakayama gives generation in the fibre local ring, and the last assertion of F.57 makes this very list regular there.

Set $T=P/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ and $J=\ker(T\to S)$. The polynomial ring is Noetherian by S01, Lemma 1.3, so $J$ is finite. Localize the short exact sequence at $\mathfrak q'$ as $P$-modules: $$ 0\longrightarrow J_{\mathfrak q'}\longrightarrow T_{\mathfrak q'}\longrightarrow S_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow0. $$ These are $R_{\mathfrak p}$-modules. Flatness of the last module makes tensoring with $k$ injective on the first arrow, by the tensor-kernel calculation S01, Lemma 1.2 and Lemma 1.A. The last arrow becomes an isomorphism after tensoring, because the chosen fibre equations generate the localized fibre ideal. Hence $$ J_{\mathfrak q'}/\mathfrak pJ_{\mathfrak q'}=0. $$ Over the local polynomial ring $P_{\mathfrak q'}$, the ideal $\mathfrak pP_{\mathfrak q'}$ is contained in its maximal ideal. Applying F.10 to the finite module $J_{\mathfrak q'}$ gives zero. Clear annihilating denominators for a finite generating list of $J$: some $u\in P\setminus\mathfrak q'$ gives $J_u=0$, and thus $T_u=S_u$.

The fibre of $T$ at the induced prime has the same local quotient by the chosen regular list. F.57 gives its point dimension $n-c$. Applying F.66(3) to this $c$-equation presentation produces a relative global complete-intersection principal neighbourhood of that point. Apply this to $T_u$, using its presentation with the additional equation $uz-1$; the fibre point dimension remains $n-c$, and the variable and equation counts both increase by one. The resulting neighbourhood is therefore a principal localization of $S_u$ with a relative global complete-intersection presentation. Writing its inverted element as a fraction in $S_u$ makes the composite neighbourhood $S_g$ for some $g\notin\mathfrak q$. This is (2). Empty regular lists use the same argument with $c=0$. ∎

Lemma F.88: syntomic presentation ideal mod squares

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07BT.

Let $R$ be Noetherian, let $S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I$ with $I$ finitely generated, and suppose $S_g$ is syntomic over $R$. Then $(I/I^2)_g$ is finite projective over $S_g$.

Proof. Put $A=S_g$ and $M=(I/I^2)_g$. If $A=0$, then $M=0$ and the assertion follows. Otherwise $A$ is Noetherian by S01, Lemma 1.3 and localization, so the finite module $M$ is finitely presented.

At every prime of $A$, F.87 supplies a principal relative global complete-intersection neighbourhood. F.77 makes the conormal of its displayed equations finite free. The presentation comparison F.33 identifies $M$ there, up to finite free summands, with that conormal. Therefore $M$ is finite projective there: the comparison realizes it as a summand of a finite free module. Choose finitely many of these neighbourhoods $D(a_i)$ covering $\operatorname{Spec}A$. The finite choice follows from the principal-open cover criterion: the ideal of all covering elements is not contained in any prime, hence contains $1$, which is a finite sum.

Here is the global splitting argument. Choose a finite free surjection $\pi:A^N\to M$. Its localization on $D(a_i)$ has a right inverse $s_i$, because $M_{a_i}$ is projective. A finite presentation $A^r\to A^s\to M\to0$ realizes $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,A^N)$ as the kernel of a map between finite matrix modules. Localization is exact and commutes with these finite modules, so $$ \operatorname{Hom}_A(M,A^N)_{a_i} =\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{a_i}}(M_{a_i},A_{a_i}^N). $$ Consequently some global $t_i:M\to A^N$ represents $a_i^{k_i}s_i$. The map $\pi t_i-a_i^{k_i}1_M$ becomes zero after inverting $a_i$. Multiplying by another power of $a_i$ kills its values on all members of a finite generating list of $M$. Replacing $t_i$ by that multiple gives $$ \pi t_i=a_i^{e_i}1_M. $$ The powers $a_i^{e_i}$ still generate $1$: if a proper ideal contained them, a containing prime would contain all the corresponding $a_i$, contradicting the cover. Choose $b_i$ with $\sum_i b_i a_i^{e_i}=1$. Then $\sum_i b_i t_i$ is a global right inverse of $\pi$. Thus $M$ is a direct summand of $A^N$, which proves finite projectivity. All denominator and zero-module cases are included. ∎

Lemma F.89: total ring fractions no embedded points

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 02LX.

Suppose a ring $R$ has finitely many minimal primes $\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_t$, and its zerodivisors are exactly their union. Its total ring of fractions has the canonical decomposition $$ Q(R)\cong\prod_{i=1}^t R_{\mathfrak q_i}. $$

Proof. If $t=0$, the assumed zerodivisor set is empty. A nonzero ring would make $0$ a zerodivisor, since it annihilates $1\ne0$, so $R=0$. Both its localization and the empty ring product are zero. Now assume $t>0$. Let $D$ be the multiplicative set of nonzerodivisors and put $A=D^{-1}R$. Every element of $D$ avoids every $\mathfrak q_i$, so each map $R\to R_{\mathfrak q_i}$ extends to $A$. The prime correspondence for localization identifies the primes of $A$ with primes of $R$ disjoint from $D$. Such a prime is contained in $\bigcup_i\mathfrak q_i$. By F.80 it is contained in one $\mathfrak q_i$, and minimality forces equality. Thus the primes of $A$ are precisely the extensions $\mathfrak m_i=D^{-1}\mathfrak q_i$. They are distinct and incomparable, hence all maximal.

We construct the product decomposition, including possible nilpotents. For each $i$ and $j\ne i$, choose an element in $\mathfrak m_j\setminus\mathfrak m_i$, and multiply these choices to obtain $a_i$. Then $a_i$ avoids $\mathfrak m_i$ and belongs to every other prime. For $t=1$ use the empty product $a_1=1$. Each product $a_i a_j$ for $i\ne j$ belongs to every prime, and hence is nilpotent by AG-CA-01, Theorem 1.2. Choose a common positive integer $N$ with $a_i^N a_j^N=0$ for every pair. The elements $a_i^N$ generate the unit ideal, since no prime contains all of them. Write $1=\sum_i b_i a_i^N$ and set $e_i=b_i a_i^N$. The $e_i$ are orthogonal and sum to $1$; multiplying this sum by $e_i$ gives $e_i^2=e_i$. Modulo $\mathfrak m_i$, only the $i$th summand survives, so $e_i$ is $1$ there and is zero at every other prime.

The maps $a\mapsto(e_i a)_i$ and $(u_i)_i\mapsto\sum_i u_i$ are inverse ring maps between $A$ and $\prod_i e_iA$. Each factor has only the prime induced by $\mathfrak m_i$, and is therefore local: a nonunit lies in a maximal ideal, which must be that prime. The projection $A\to e_iA$ consequently inverts every element outside $\mathfrak m_i$. Conversely, in $A_{\mathfrak m_i}$ the idempotent $e_i$ is a unit and hence equals $1$, so the complementary factor vanishes. These universal properties give $e_iA\cong A_{\mathfrak m_i}\cong R_{\mathfrak q_i}$. The isomorphism is the canonical map stated above. ∎

Lemma F.90: when colimit

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07C3.

For an arbitrary ring map $R\to\Lambda$, the following are equivalent: $\Lambda$ is a filtered colimit of smooth $R$-algebras; every $R$-algebra map from a finitely presented algebra $A$ to $\Lambda$ factors through a smooth $R$-algebra.

Proof. First suppose such a filtered presentation of $\Lambda$ is given. Write $A$ with finitely many polynomial generators and finitely many defining equations. The images of its generators have representatives at a common stage. Each defining equation becomes zero at a later stage, by the equality criterion in a filtered colimit. A common successor of those finitely many stages therefore satisfies every equation. The generator images define the required map to that smooth stage.

For the converse, form the category whose objects are smooth $R$-algebras $B$ with a map $B\to\Lambda$, and whose arrows commute with those maps. Smooth algebras are finitely presented. This category can be taken small: finite polynomial presentations form a set, and a map from each one to $\Lambda$ is specified by a finite tuple of elements of $\Lambda$; use these presentations as representatives. The object $R\to\Lambda$ makes it nonempty.

Given two objects $B_1,B_2$, the tensor product $B_1\otimes_R B_2$ is finitely presented: combine their finite generator lists and equations. Factor its induced map to $\Lambda$ through a smooth algebra. The two structure maps into that algebra give a common successor in the category. For parallel arrows $u,v\colon B\rightrightarrows C$, choose finite algebra generators $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ of $B$. The quotient $$ C/(u(b_1)-v(b_1),\ldots,u(b_r)-v(b_r)) $$ is finitely presented by adding these finitely many equations to a presentation of $C$. Its map to $\Lambda$ factors through a smooth algebra by the hypothesis. The resulting arrow from $C$ equalizes $u$ and $v$, because equality on the generators gives equality on every polynomial in them. These two constructions prove filteredness.

Let $L$ be this category's colimit and $L\to\Lambda$ its induced map. It is surjective: for any $\lambda\in\Lambda$, apply the factoring hypothesis to $R[T]\to\Lambda$ with $T\mapsto\lambda$; the intermediate object supplies a representative of $\lambda$ in $L$. For injectivity, a representative $b\in B$ with zero image in $\Lambda$ gives a map $B/(b)\to\Lambda$. This quotient is finitely presented, so its factorization through a smooth object yields a successor at which $b=0$. Hence its colimit class is zero. Two representatives can be moved to a common stage and this argument applied to their difference, proving equality detection as well. Thus $L\to\Lambda$ is an isomorphism of $R$-algebras, establishing the filtered presentation without any Noetherian hypothesis. ∎

Proposition F.91: characterize separable field extensions

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 46037–46069.

For every field extension $K/k$, the following are equivalent: separability in F.5; geometric reducedness over $k$; algebraic formal smoothness over $k$; $H_1(L_{K/k})=0$; and injectivity of $$\iota:K\otimes_k\Omega_{k/P}\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/P},$$ where $P$ is the prime field. In characteristic $p>0$ they are also equivalent to the condition that an absolute $p$-basis of $k$ remains $p$-independent over $K^p$. In characteristic zero all the conditions hold. For finitely generated extensions they agree with the existence of a separating transcendence basis.

Proof. We give the comparisons in an order that does not assume the last finitely generated assertion.

First, every field is formally smooth over its prime field. In characteristic zero, choose a transcendence basis over $\mathbf Q$; the remaining algebraic extension is separable, because a nonconstant irreducible polynomial has nonzero derivative of smaller degree and hence is relatively prime to it. The two entire lifting constructions in F.49, together with the composition lifting proof AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2, give formal smoothness, for arbitrary bases and algebraic extensions.

In characteristic $p$, take an absolute $p$-basis $B$ of a field $H$ by the whole F.119. Given a prime-field map $\psi:H\to D/J$, $J^2=0$, define a lift on $H^p$ by $$\theta(a^p)=\widetilde{\psi(a)}^{\,p}.$$ The root $a$ is unique in $H$, and changing its chosen lift by $j\in J$ does not change this power, since $j^p=0$. Frobenius of sums and products proves that $\theta$ is a unital ring map. Choose arbitrary lifts of the $\psi(b)$ for $b\in B$. Their $p$th powers are $\theta(b^p)$; the exact presentation $$H=H^p[T_b:b\in B]/(T_b^p-b^p)$$ proved in F.119 therefore extends them to a lift on $H$. This establishes prime-field formal smoothness in both characteristics.

Suppose $\iota$ is injective. In a square-zero lifting problem for $K/k$, obtain a $P$-lift $u:K\to D$ by the preceding argument. Write $v:k\to D$ for the prescribed structural map. The difference $u|_k-v$ takes values in $J$ and is a $P$-derivation for the common action modulo $J$, by expanding a product and using $J^2=0$. The given map $K\to D/J$ makes $J$ a $K$-vector space. Its derivation corresponds to a linear map from $K\otimes_k\Omega_{k/P}$ to $J$; extend it along the injection $\iota$ to $\Omega_{K/P}$ by extending a vector-space basis. The resulting derivation $\delta:K\to J$ gives the corrected lift $u-\delta$. Indeed $$ (u(x)-\delta(x))(u(y)-\delta(y)) =u(xy)-u(x)\delta(y)-u(y)\delta(x) =u(xy)-\delta(xy). $$ It preserves one and agrees with $v$ on $k$, proving formal smoothness.

Conversely, any $P$-derivation $d:k\to V$, for a $K$-vector space $V$, makes $K\oplus V$ a $k$-algebra by $a\mapsto(a,d(a))$; its multiplication is $(x,v)(y,w)=(xy,xw+yv)$. Formal smoothness lifts the identity through the square-zero quotient to $K$. The second component of that lift is a derivation extending $d$. Thus every linear functional on the domain of $\iota$ extends to its codomain. If a nonzero vector lay in its kernel, extend that vector to a basis and take a functional equal to one on it; such a functional could not extend. Hence $\iota$ is injective. The whole F.17 proves precisely the equivalence with the displayed first cotangent homology condition, in arbitrary field scope.

In characteristic $p$, F.119 identifies the differentials of an absolute $p$-basis $B$ of $k$ with a basis of $\Omega_{k/P}$. Applied over $P$ to $K$, its other equivalence says their images are independent exactly when the standard monomials in $B$ are independent over $K^p$. This proves the equivalence with $\iota$'s injectivity.

We next compare this condition with reducedness. A finite root algebra $$K\otimes_k k(b^{1/p}:b\in B_0) =K[T_b:b\in B_0]/(T_b^p-b),\qquad B_0\subset B\ {\rm finite},$$ is free on the standard monomials. The corresponding root-field monomials are independent over $K$ exactly when the monomials in $B_0$ are independent over $K^p$: raise a proposed relation to its $p$th power, and take roots of its coefficients for the converse. If independent, the algebra maps isomorphically to the root field. If dependent, that map has a nonzero kernel. Every element of the root algebra has $p$th power in $K$; a kernel element therefore has $p$th power zero in the algebra itself. It is a nonzero nilpotent. The full algebra $K\otimes_k k^{1/p}$ is the union of these algebras with injective transitions, since a full $p$-basis expansion expresses every root using finitely many basis roots. Reducedness of this union is equivalent to reducedness of every finite stage. Thus geometric reducedness implies the $p$-basis condition.

For the converse we must test all field extensions. The independence persists through all root heights. More explicitly, a relation $$\sum_a c_a^{p^r}B^a=0,\qquad 0\leq a_b<p^r,$$ can be grouped by $a=pu+v$, $0\leq v_b<p$. The coefficient of $B^v$ is $$\left(\sum_u c_{pu+v}^{p^{r-1}}B^u\right)^p.$$ Independence over $K^p$ makes each coefficient zero. Frobenius is injective in a field; induction on $r$ then kills every $c_a$. Iterating the unique finite $p$-basis expansions in $k$ shows that the monomials with exponents below $p^r$ are a basis of $k$ over $k^{p^r}$. Taking roots gives the standard presentation and basis of every finite subset root extension of height $r$. The preceding relation calculation makes all its base changes to $K$ fields; their directed union $K\otimes_k k^{1/p^r}$ is a field too.

Every finite purely inseparable extension $k'/k$ embeds over $k$ in some $k^{1/p^r}$: choose finitely many generators and a common root height. Tensoring its inclusion with the vector space $K$ is injective. Hence $K\otimes_k k'$ is a finite-dimensional domain over $K$, and is a field by the multiplication-inverse argument.

Now take a finitely generated field extension $E/k$. In characteristic $p$, the entire F.69 supplies finite purely inseparable $k'/k$, an extension $E'/E$ containing $k'$, and a separating transcendence basis for $E'/k'$. Put $H=K\otimes_k k'$, a field as just proved. In characteristic zero use $k'=k$, $H=K$ and $E'=E$: a maximal algebraically independent subset of finite field generators leaves a finite algebraic, necessarily separable, extension.

In either case, for a separating basis $T$, the ring $$C=H\otimes_{k'}k'(T)=\bigl(k'[T]\setminus\{0\}\bigr)^{-1}H[T]$$ is a domain. The algebra $C\otimes_{k'(T)}E'$ is finite free over $C$, by a vector-space basis of the finite separable field extension $E'/k'(T)$. It therefore injects into its localization over $\operatorname{Frac}(C)$. That generic algebra is reduced: express the finite separable extension by a finite tower of simple generators. At each step a monic minimal polynomial is relatively prime to its derivative, and its Bézout identity remains valid after any field extension. Its irreducible factors are consequently distinct. The two-factor Bézout Chinese remainder formula and its finite induction, proved in F.73, identify its quotient with a product of fields. Repeat on every field factor at the next step of the tower. The final tensor algebra is a finite product of fields, hence reduced. Its subalgebra $C\otimes E'=H\otimes_{k'}E'=K\otimes_kE'$ is reduced as well.

The inclusion $E\subset E'$ remains injective after tensoring over $k$ with $K$, since field-vector-space inclusions split by extending bases. Thus $K\otimes_kE$ is reduced. An arbitrary field extension of $k$ is the directed union of its finitely generated subfields, with injective tensor transitions. A nilpotent and its finite power relation occur at one stage, so the union is reduced. This proves geometric reducedness from the $p$-basis condition; it also proves it for all extensions in characteristic zero.

It remains to connect formal smoothness with the definition of separability. For a finitely generated formally smooth field $L/k$, choose a finite-type domain $B=k[a_1,\ldots,a_n]\subset L$ with fraction field $L$, and a polynomial presentation $Q=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\to B$ with prime kernel $I$. Hilbert's basis theorem AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, makes $I$ finite. The entire localization comparison F.65, together with F.17 for $L/k$, makes $$ (I/I^2)\otimes_B L\longrightarrow L^n $$ injective: exact field-of-fractions localization identifies this map's kernel with the localized first cotangent homology. Choose $f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I$ whose conormal classes form a basis of this finite-dimensional space. Their differentials are independent, giving a $c$-column Jacobian determinant $\Delta\notin I$.

The local ring $Q_I$ has maximal ideal $IQ_I$ and residue field $L$. Its cotangent space is exactly the conormal space just used. The whole F.10 makes the $f_i$ generate $IQ_I$. The finite module $I/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ then vanishes there. Kill its finite generator list by a product $h_0\notin I$ of annihilating denominators. For $h=h_0\Delta$ and its image $g\in B$ this gives $$B_g=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n,Z]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,hZ-1).$$ The square Jacobian block using the selected columns and $Z$ has determinant $h\Delta$, a unit. The full AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1, makes this a standard smooth domain. Its fraction field is $L$, and the entire domain calculation F.64 gives a separating transcendence basis. This includes $c=0$, with empty minor one. Conversely such a basis gives a purely transcendental extension followed by a finite separable one; F.49 and the full formal composition proof make $L/k$ formally smooth.

If $K/k$ is separable by F.5, the whole F.49(3) gives formal smoothness, hence the conditions already compared. Conversely, in characteristic $p$ the $p$-basis condition descends to every finitely generated intermediate $L$: coefficients in $L^p$ are also in $K^p$. The differential and lifting comparisons make $L/k$ formally smooth, and the preceding finite construction makes it separably generated. This is exactly F.5's definition for $K/k$. In characteristic zero the finite transcendence-basis argument above gives that definition for every intermediate field. Finally F.49 gives formal smoothness there, hence differential injectivity and the homology condition. All comparisons and the finite-generation assertion are now proved. ∎

Definition F.92: G ring

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07GH.

The term G-ring imposes two requirements on $R$: it is Noetherian, and at every prime $\mathfrak p$ its localization-to-completion map is regular. The map in this second requirement is $$ R_{\mathfrak p}\longrightarrow\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}, \qquad \widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}} =\varprojlim_{n\ge1}R_{\mathfrak p}/(\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p})^n. $$ Thus the completion used in the definition is taken at the maximal ideal of the local ring, separately for each prime.

Definition F.93: excellent

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07QT.

For a Noetherian ring $R$, quasi-excellence means that $R$ satisfies the G-ring condition of F.92 and the J-2 condition. Here J-2 requires the regular locus $$ \{\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}B:B_{\mathfrak q}\text{ is regular}\} $$ to be open for each finite-type $R$-algebra $B$; this is the terminology of Stacks, Tag 07P7.

An excellent ring has these properties and is universally catenary. To specify that last condition, a ring is catenary when, between each fixed pair of comparable primes, the lengths of finite strict chains have a common finite bound and the chains into which no further prime can be inserted all have equal length. A Noetherian ring is universally catenary when every finite-type algebra over it has this property. These two definitions are Stacks, Tag 00NI and Tag 00NL.

Definition F.94: local complete intersection

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07D0.

For a map $A\to B$ of finite type, choose a surjection $$ P=A[T_1,\ldots,T_n]\twoheadrightarrow B, \qquad I=\ker(P\to B). $$ The map is a local complete intersection when $I$ is a Koszul-regular ideal, with that ideal condition understood exactly as in F.95. Checking one such presentation suffices: the full arbitrary-ring proof F.94.A below shows that every other finite polynomial presentation then has a Koszul-regular kernel. Neither this definition nor that comparison assumes $A$ Noetherian.

Lemma F.94.A: arbitrary-ring presentation independence

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 8869–8942; Stacks, Tag 07CZ.

Let $A$ be an arbitrary ring and suppose an algebra $C$ has finite polynomial presentations $$P=A[T_1,\ldots,T_n]\twoheadrightarrow C=P/I,\qquad Q=A[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\twoheadrightarrow C=Q/J.$$ If $I$ is a Koszul-regular ideal as defined in F.95, then $J$ is also Koszul-regular. Moreover $C$ is finitely presented. This proves the presentation-independence assertion in F.94 without Noetherian hypotheses.

Proof. We first supply the elementary complex calculations used to compare the two presentations.

For a list $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ over a ring $V$, take a free module with basis $e_1,\ldots,e_c$ and form $$K_j(f;V)=\bigwedge^jV^c,\qquad d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_j}) =\sum_{a=1}^j(-1)^{a-1}f_{i_a} e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_a}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_j}.$$ Deleting a pair of indices in the two orders gives opposite signs, so $d^2=0$. Its degree-zero homology is $V/(f)$. Appending $u$ identifies the new degree-$j$ term with $K_j(f)\oplus K_{j-1}(f)$, with differential $$d(a,b)=(d_fa+ub,-d_fb);$$ the sign identification multiplies the wedge ending in the added basis vector by $(-1)^{j-1}$.

If $K(f)$ has zero positive homology and $u$ acts injectively on $V/(f)$, this cone has zero positive homology too. Indeed a degree-$j$ cycle satisfies $d_fb=0$ and $d_fa=-ub$. For $j>1$, write $b=d_fc$ using the old acyclicity. For $j=1$, the last equation makes $u[b]=0$ in $H_0(K(f))$; injectivity likewise gives $b=d_fc$. Subtract the boundary of $(0,-c)$ to obtain $(a+uc,0)$, an old positive-degree cycle. Its old bounding chain makes this remaining vector a boundary in the cone. Degree zero is the additional quotient by $u$. This proves the appending assertion, including empty initial lists.

A second calculation will detect conormal ranks. If $H_1(K(f))=0$, the classes of the $f_i$ give a basis of $(f)/(f)^2$ over $V/(f)$. They generate by definition. Given $\sum_i b_if_i\in(f)^2$, write the right side as $\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}f_if_j$ and replace $b_i$ by $b_i-\sum_j a_{ij}f_j$. Their scalar product is now exactly zero, so the resulting vector is a degree-one cycle. A degree-two Koszul boundary has every coordinate in $(f)$. Vanishing of $H_1$ therefore puts all the corrected coefficients, and hence every $b_i$, in $(f)$. This proves independence.

We next prove that the kernels are finite. The principal charts in the Koszul-regularity condition cover $V(I)$. If their denominators are $a_\lambda\in P$, then $I+(a_\lambda)=P$: a proper ideal is contained in a maximal ideal, which would give an uncovered prime containing $I$. Thus finitely many denominators and an element $b\in I$ satisfy $$1=b+\sum_{\ell=1}^s c_\ell a_\ell.$$ Choose numerators in $I$ of every finite local generator list for $I_{a_\ell}$, and let $I_0$ be generated by those numerators and $b$. At a prime where some $a_\ell$ is invertible, $I_0$ and $I$ have the same localization. At any other prime, the identity makes $b$ a unit, so both localize to the unit ideal. Therefore $(I/I_0)$ vanishes at every prime, and is zero. Here is local detection for this possibly infinite module: a nonzero element has a proper annihilator contained in a maximal ideal; if it became zero there, an element outside that ideal would annihilate it, a contradiction. Hence $I=I_0$ is finite. This makes $C$ finitely presented, and the entire F.44 then makes $J$ finite. If $C=0$, both kernels are unit ideals and their required prime tests are empty. We now assume $C\ne0$ and fix $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}C$.

Choose $p_j(T)\in P$ representing each image of $X_j$ and $q_i(X)\in Q$ representing each image of $T_i$. In $W=A[T,X]$ the kernel $L$ of the common map to $C$ has two exact descriptions: $$L=(I,u_1,\ldots,u_m)=(J,s_1,\ldots,s_n),\qquad u_j=X_j-p_j(T),\quad s_i=T_i-q_i(X).$$ Quotienting by the added equations eliminates those variables and recovers the specified maps to $C$, which proves both descriptions. Let $\mathfrak r\subset W$ be the inverse image of $\mathfrak q$, and $\mathfrak p_P,\mathfrak p_Q$ its contractions. Translation is a polynomial-ring isomorphism $W=Q[s_1,\ldots,s_n]$. Constant and linear coefficients in these variables give an exact decomposition $$L/L^2=(J/J^2)\oplus C^n.$$ The constant part is taken modulo $J^2$, the linear coefficients modulo $J$, and all terms with at least two $s$ factors disappear. Sending these data to their constant-plus-linear representatives and reading them back gives inverse maps, so the decomposition is valid over arbitrary rings.

Pick $a\in P\setminus\mathfrak p_P$ and a Koszul-regular list $f$ generating $I_a$. Polynomial extension is free and localization is flat, by the entire tensor/localization proofs AG-RG-S01, Lemmas 1.0–1.1; exact flat tensor preserves each cycle and boundary quotient of this complex. Hence $f$ remains Koszul-regular over $W_a$. In the quotient by $f$, the $u_j$ are successive polynomial variables after translation. Multiplication by each is injective by comparison of coefficients, and remains so after localization. Applying the cone calculation one entry at a time proves that $(f,u)$ is Koszul-regular over $W_a$. Its conormal classes consequently form a basis of $L/L^2$ at $\mathfrak r$.

The decomposition above now makes $(J/J^2)_{\mathfrak q}$ a finite direct summand of a finite free $C_{\mathfrak q}$-module. Such a summand is flat by restricting the free tensor injection test. It is finitely presented: the projection onto its complementary summand sends a finite free basis to finitely many generators of the kernel of the projection onto the original summand. The whole AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.2, therefore makes it finite free over this local ring.

From a finite generating list of $J$ choose $g_1,\ldots,g_d$ whose conormal residue classes form a basis. Relative to a basis of the finite free conormal module, their square coefficient matrix is invertible modulo the maximal ideal, hence has unit determinant and is invertible by the cofactor formula. They thus form a basis over $C_{\mathfrak q}$. In $Q_{\mathfrak p_Q}$ this says $J=(g)+J^2$. The finite module $J/(g)$ equals $J$ times itself; $J$ lies in the maximal ideal. The entire Nakayama proof in AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.2, gives $J_{\mathfrak p_Q}=(g)$. Since $J$ is finite, kill the finitely many quotient generators by denominators outside $\mathfrak p_Q$. Their product $v_0\notin\mathfrak p_Q$ gives $J_{v_0}=(g)$ on an actual principal chart.

In $W_{\mathfrak r}$ both $(f,u)$ and $(g,s)$ generate $L_{\mathfrak r}$ and their conormal classes are bases. Their lengths agree by reduction to the residue field. Expressing the second list in the first gives a square matrix $M$ whose reduction modulo $\mathfrak r$ is invertible: $L^2\subset\mathfrak rL$, so these are precisely the two bases of $L/\mathfrak rL$. The determinant is therefore a unit. The exterior powers of the map on free generator modules give an isomorphism of the Koszul complexes. Indeed that map preserves their degree-one scalar-product functional, so the alternating deletion formula checks commutation with $d$ on every wedge; the exterior powers of the inverse matrix give the inverse complex map. Permuting $(g,s)$ to $(s,g)$ is the same calculation with a permutation matrix.

All of this can be realized on a principal neighbourhood. Include $a$ and $v_0$ in a denominator product. Include representatives outside $\mathfrak r$ of every denominator in the finite matrix and both finite generator comparisons, and the numerator of its determinant. For each asserted equality in the stalk, also include a denominator outside $\mathfrak r$ that kills its cross-difference. Their product $h\notin\mathfrak r$ gives the actual generator equalities over $W_h$ and an invertible comparison matrix there. This clearing uses annihilating denominators and never cancels a zero divisor. The complex on $(s,g)$ over $W_h$ is consequently isomorphic to the acyclic-positive complex on $(f,u)$.

Evaluate $h$ by $T_i=q_i(X)$, and call the resulting element of $Q$ $v$. Its image in $C$ agrees with that of $h$, so $v\notin\mathfrak p_Q$. Elimination and localization give $$W_h/(s)=Q_v,\qquad J_v=(g).$$ The second equality holds because $v_0$ was a factor of $h$, and hence of $v$.

Finally $K(s;W_h)$ is a free resolution of $Q_v$. Before localization this follows by appending the successive polynomial variables $s_i$ with the cone calculation above; exact localization preserves it. Form its double complex with the finite free complex $K(g;W_h)$. The total complex is $K(s,g;W_h)$, with differential $d_s+(-1)^i d_g$ at $s$-degree $i$. Augmentation maps it to $K(g;Q_v)$ and induces an isomorphism on homology. To verify this without a spectral sequence, augment each vertical column by its quotient in degree $-1$. Every such column is exact because the fixed $g$ term is free. For a total cycle, its component of greatest $g$ degree is a vertical cycle: no component of greater $g$ degree contributes to its differential. Lift it in that exact column and subtract the resulting total boundary. This removes that component and changes only smaller $g$ degrees. The procedure terminates, because there are only finitely many $g$ degrees. It proves the augmented total complex acyclic, equivalently both surjectivity and injectivity of the augmentation on homology by lifting cycles and boundaries.

The source total complex has zero positive homology. Thus $K(g;Q_v)$ does too, and its entries generate $J_v$. We have produced the required Koszul-regular principal neighbourhood of the specified prime of $C$. Repeating for every prime proves the claim for $J$. The equations, complexes and finite eliminations include all empty variable and generator lists. ∎

Definition F.95: regular ideal

Reading sources: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 8710–8731; Stacks, Tag 061P.

Let $R$ be any ring. For a finite list $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ put $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$.

  1. The list is regular when $J\ne R$ and multiplication by $f_i$ is injective on $R/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})$ for every $i$.
  2. It is Koszul-regular when every positive-degree homology module of the exterior-power Koszul complex $K(f;R)$ is zero.
  3. It is $H_1$-regular when $H_1(K(f;R))=0$.
  4. It is quasi-regular when the graded $R/J$-algebra map $$ (R/J)[Z_1,\ldots,Z_c]\longrightarrow \operatorname{gr}_J(R)=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}J^d/J^{d+1}, \quad Z_1^{e_1}\cdots Z_c^{e_c}\longmapsto f_1^{e_1}\cdots f_c^{e_c}\bmod J^{1+\sum_i e_i} $$ is an isomorphism.

For an ideal $I\subset R$, each of these four conditions defines the corresponding regular, Koszul-regular, $H_1$-regular, or quasi-regular ideal by the following local requirement: for every prime $\mathfrak p$ containing $I$, there are $g\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ and a finite list in $R_g$ generating $I_g$ and satisfying that list condition. The denominator and list may depend on the prime. This specifies all four ideal definitions over arbitrary rings.

Verification of the formulas. The complex in (2) and (3) has term $\bigwedge^dR^c$ and differential $$ d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_d}) =\sum_{a=1}^d(-1)^{a-1}f_{i_a} e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_a}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_d}. $$ Each pair of deleted indices contributes twice to $d^2$, with opposite signs, so this is a complex in every characteristic. Its degree-zero homology is $R/J$, since the degree-one differential has image $J$. The whole complex calculations in F.94.A also apply to the empty list.

The map in (4) is well defined on coefficients modulo $J$: changing a coefficient by an element of $J$ changes a degree-$d$ value by an element of $J^{d+1}$. Multiplication of representatives respects the displayed graded products, so it is a graded algebra map. It is surjective in every degree because $J^d$ is generated by the degree-$d$ products of the $f_i$. If it is an isomorphism, degree one gives precisely $$ (R/J)^c\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}J/J^2, \qquad (a_i)\longmapsto\sum_i a_if_i\bmod J^2. $$ Thus quasi-regularity includes the conormal basis used later.

For the empty list $J=0$, the complex consists only of $R$ in degree zero and the graded map is the identity of $R$ in degree zero. It supplies all four local tests for the zero ideal at its primes. For $I=R$, no prime contains it and the ideal conditions are vacuous. These conventions handle both the zero ring and empty charts without a Noetherian hypothesis. ∎

Lemma F.96: G ring goes up quasi finite

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12823–12870.

Let $R\to R'$ be finite type between Noetherian rings. Let $\mathfrak q'\subset\mathfrak p'$ be primes of $R'$ contracting to $\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p$ in $R$, and assume the map is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak p'$.

  1. If $\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is geometrically regular over $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, then $\widehat{R'_{\mathfrak p'}}\otimes_{R'}\kappa(\mathfrak q')$ is geometrically regular over $\kappa(\mathfrak q')$.
  2. If all formal fibres of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ are geometrically regular, the same holds for $R'_{\mathfrak p'}$.
  3. A quasi-finite algebra over a Noetherian G-ring is a G-ring.

Proof. Put $A=\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}$, $B=\widehat{R'_{\mathfrak p'}}$, $k=\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ and $E=\kappa(\mathfrak q')$. The ring $A$ is Noetherian by AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.3, and $T$ is a finite-type $A$-algebra, hence Noetherian by the earlier Hilbert basis theorem. The completion map is flat by AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.2, so these fibres make it regular. For (3), quasi-finiteness applies at every $\mathfrak p'$, and the G-ring hypothesis gives the assumption of (2) at its contracted $\mathfrak p$. Lemma F.97: another helper G ring

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 13103–13159.

Let $R$ be a complete Noetherian local domain with fraction field $K$. For every prime $\mathfrak q\subset R[X]$, the ring $\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q}}\otimes_RK$ is regular. Moreover, if $\mathfrak q$ lies over the maximal ideal of $R$ and $0\ne\mathfrak r\subset\mathfrak q$ contracts to zero in $R$, then $$\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q}}\otimes_{R[X]}\kappa(\mathfrak r)$$ is geometrically regular over $\kappa(\mathfrak r)$. The second assertion includes the maximal-ideal, positive-characteristic case of the reading source.

Therefore $R\otimes_{A_0}F$ is a field containing $R$ and equals $K$. In particular $K/F$ is finite.

Applying F.27 to the finite map $A_0[X]\to R[X]$ gives $$\widehat{A_0[X]_{\mathfrak q_0}}\otimes_{A_0[X]}R[X] \cong\prod_i\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q_i}},$$ where the finitely many $\mathfrak q_i$ are all primes above $\mathfrak q_0$, including $\mathfrak q$. Its tensor with $K$ is Noetherian, since $K/F$ is finite, and is regular by F.52. On the right it is the product of the rings $\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q_i}}\otimes_RK$. Each factor is localization of that product at its factor idempotent, so its local rings are regular and it is Noetherian. This proves the first assertion for every prime, without a formal-smoothness criterion for regularity.

For the second assertion set $E=\kappa(\mathfrak r)$. The prime $\mathfrak r$ remains nonzero in $K[X]$: choose a nonzero polynomial in it, and localization is injective because $R[X]$ is a domain. Its extension is a proper prime, by the localization correspondence, and hence is generated by an irreducible polynomial of positive degree in the Euclidean ring $K[X]$. Thus $E=K[X]/\mathfrak rK[X]$ is finite over $K$. The equality with the residue field follows because this quotient is already a field containing the image of $R[X]/\mathfrak r$ and all its fractions.

Fix a finite purely inseparable extension $L/E$. It is finite over $K$. Choose finitely many algebraic field generators of $L/K$ and multiply each by a nonzero element of $R$ so that its monic equation has coefficients in $R$: for a degree-$d$ equation, the coefficient of degree $j$ is multiplied by the $(d-j)$th power of that scalar. The resulting integral generators define a finite domain $B\subset L$, $R\subset B$, with fraction field $L$. The ring $B$ is complete local, as follows directly from F.27 applied to the complete ring $R$ at its maximal ideal. Its left side is $B$, so $$B\cong\prod_j\widehat{B_{\mathfrak n_j}}.$$ Integral maximal-ideal correspondence makes the $\mathfrak n_j$ exactly its maximal ideals. Each factor is nonzero, since its residue-field quotient is nonzero. A domain has only the idempotents zero and one: $e(1-e)=0$ proves this. Hence there is exactly one factor. The resulting unique maximal ideal makes $B=B_{\mathfrak n}$, and the natural isomorphism identifies it with its maximal-adic completion. Finiteness over Noetherian $R$ also makes $B$ Noetherian.

Let $a\in L$ be the image of $X$ through $R[X]\to E\to L$, and let $\mathfrak r'=\ker(B[X]\to L)$ for the map evaluating $X$ at $a$. The quotient image is a domain containing $B$, so its fraction field contains $\operatorname{Frac}(B)=L$ and equals $L$. Thus $\kappa(\mathfrak r')=L$, and $\mathfrak r'$ contracts to $\mathfrak r$ in $R[X]$. Its extension to $L[X]$ is exactly $(X-a)$.
