In each factor tensor first with $L=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ over $B$ and then impose the evaluation relation in $L[X]$. Its ring is precisely $$\bigl(\widehat{B[X]_{\mathfrak q_i}}\otimes_BL\bigr)/(X-a).$$ The parent ring is Noetherian regular by the already proved first assertion, applied to the complete local domain $B$ and the prime $\mathfrak q_i$; no maximality assumption on this prime is needed. Polynomial differentiation $\partial/\partial X$ kills $B$. The three successive extensions through prime localization, completion and localization by $B\setminus\{0\}$ are furnished by F.104. Its fraction formula shows that it kills $L$ as well, and it sends $X-a$ to one. The full hypersurface argument F.122 therefore makes this quotient regular. A zero quotient is included. A finite product of regular Noetherian rings is regular: each prime contains all but one factor idempotent and its local ring is the corresponding factor local ring. The tested fibre is consequently regular for every $L/E$. It is Noetherian as a localized quotient of $H$ before the finite field extension. Criterion F.50 proves the claimed geometric regularity. ∎

Lemma F.98: cartier equality

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07E1.

For a finitely generated field extension $K/k$, the spaces of differentials and first conormal homology are finite-dimensional, and $$ \dim_K\Omega_{K/k}-\dim_K H_1(L_{K/k}) =\operatorname{trdeg}_k K. $$

Proof. Put $d=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K$. Apply the explicit monic-tower construction in F.23 to a finite field-generating list for $K/k$. It gives a domain $C\subset K$ containing that list and having fraction field $K$. In that construction there are $d$ transcendence variables, $r$ algebraic tower variables and one inverse variable. Consequently its polynomial presentation has $$ N=d+r+1\quad\text{variables},\qquad c=r+1\quad\text{equations}. $$ The first equation is $hZ-1$ for the chosen nonzero denominator polynomial $h$. The remaining equations, after imposing this first equation, are the successive monic minimal polynomials in the tower. Multiplication by $hZ-1$ is injective: the lowest nonzero coefficient of a polynomial in its product with $hZ-1$ is the negative of that coefficient. Each subsequent monic equation is injective on its polynomial ring by its highest-coefficient calculation. Thus this ordered list is regular, exactly as in the construction of F.23.

Write $C=k[X_1,\ldots,X_N]/I$. F.74 identifies $I/I^2$ with $C^c$ on the equation classes. Polynomial differentials identify the other term with $C^N$ on $dX_i$. Presentation comparison F.11 and localization F.65, applied at all nonzero elements of the domain $C$, therefore identify the first conormal homology and the differential module of $K/k$ with the kernel and cokernel of a linear map $$ D:K^c\longrightarrow K^N. $$ Localization is exact by S01, Lemma 1.1, so it preserves the kernel and cokernel used in this comparison.

If $\rho$ is the rank of $D$, choosing bases for its image and extending them to bases gives $$ \dim_K\ker D=c-\rho,\qquad \dim_K\operatorname{coker}D=N-\rho. $$ Their difference is $N-c=d$, and both numbers are finite. This proves the asserted equality without a separability hypothesis. Equivalently the parameter count is $\dim C=d=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K$, as proved for finite-type domains in AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.2. Empty transcendence or tower lists obey the same count, including $K=k$. ∎

Lemma F.99: check G ring easy

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12803–12821.

A Noetherian ring $R$ is a G-ring exactly when, for every pair of primes $\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p$, the algebra $$ \widehat{(R/\mathfrak q)_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_{R/\mathfrak q}\kappa(\mathfrak q) $$ is geometrically regular over $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. The completion is at the maximal ideal of the displayed local quotient.

Proof. Fix $\mathfrak p$ and put $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak pA$. Primes of $A$ correspond exactly to primes $\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p$ of $R$, by extension and contraction in localization. Their residue fields are the same $\kappa(\mathfrak q)=\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak q)$: tensoring with that field already inverts every denominator outside $\mathfrak p$.

Since $A$ is Noetherian, both $\mathfrak qA$ and $A/\mathfrak qA$ are finite $A$-modules. The whole completion exactness and tensor theorem AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.1 applied to $$0\longrightarrow\mathfrak qA\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow A/\mathfrak qA\longrightarrow0$$ gives the natural ring identification $$ \widehat A/\mathfrak q\widehat A \ \cong\ \widehat{A/\mathfrak qA} =\widehat{(R/\mathfrak q)_{\mathfrak p}}. $$ The completion topology on the quotient is the correct maximal-ideal topology: its degree-$r$ quotient is $A/(\mathfrak m^r+\mathfrak qA)$. The kernel image is $\mathfrak q\widehat A$, since the tensor map from the finite ideal sends its generators and coefficients to their products in $\widehat A$.

Because $\mathfrak q$ annihilates $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, the defining balanced tensor relations now give $$ \widehat A\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak q) \cong \widehat A\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak q) \cong(\widehat A/\mathfrak q\widehat A)\otimes_{R/\mathfrak q}\kappa(\mathfrak q). $$ Explicitly the last map sends $\widehat a\otimes\lambda$ to $(\widehat a\bmod\mathfrak q\widehat A)\otimes\lambda$. Its inverse chooses a representative; changing the representative adds products by elements of $\mathfrak q$, whose tensors vanish. The first identity holds because the inverted denominators act invertibly in both factors. These maps preserve the specified residue-field algebra structures.

The entire AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.2, makes $A\to\widehat A$ flat. Thus it is regular precisely when all its residue-field fibres are geometrically regular, by the regular-map definition. The identities above identify those fibres with exactly the algebras in the assertion. By F.92, being a G-ring means that this regularity holds at every $\mathfrak p$. Applying the equivalence at each prime proves both directions. If $R=0$, there are no primes and the two conditions are vacuous. ∎

Lemma F.99A: completion of a flat local map

Reading sources: AG-CA-19, Proposition 2.2 and Theorems 3.2–3.3; AG-CA-08, Theorems 4.2 and 2.1.

If $(A,\mathfrak m)\to(B,\mathfrak n)$ is a flat local map of Noetherian local rings, its induced map on maximal-ideal completions $\widehat A\to\widehat B$ is faithfully flat. The residue fields may differ.

Proof. Since $\mathfrak m^r$ maps into $\mathfrak n^r$, the finite-quotient maps $A/\mathfrak m^r\to B/\mathfrak n^r$ commute with their transitions. Their inverse limit defines the asserted map.

The entire completion proofs AG-CA-19, Proposition 2.2 and Theorem 3.3, make the completions Noetherian and complete, with $$\widehat A/\mathfrak m\widehat A=A/\mathfrak m=\kappa, \qquad \widehat B/\mathfrak n\widehat B=B/\mathfrak n.$$ These are local rings with the indicated extended maximal ideals. Explicitly, an element whose residue is nonzero has an inverse modulo the extended ideal. Its product with a chosen inverse is $1-j$; the series $\sum_{r\geq0}j^r$ converges in the complete ring and inverts this product. Thus every element outside the extended maximal ideal is a unit. The completion map sends $\mathfrak m\widehat A$ into $\mathfrak n\widehat B$, so it is local.

Choose a free $A$-resolution $F_\bullet\to\kappa$ by the whole construction AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A. The full AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.2, proves $A\to\widehat A$ flat, so $F_\bullet\otimes_A\widehat A$ is an exact free $\widehat A$-resolution of $\kappa\otimes_A\widehat A=\kappa$. The same theorem makes $\widehat B$ flat over $B$, and the given flatness of $B/A$ then makes it flat over $A$ by tensor associativity. Consequently tensoring the original resolution with $\widehat B$ is exact in positive degrees, and $$ \operatorname{Tor}^{\widehat A}_1(\kappa,\widehat B) =H_1\bigl((F_\bullet\otimes_A\widehat A) \otimes_{\widehat A}\widehat B\bigr) =H_1(F_\bullet\otimes_A\widehat B)=0. $$

Apply the complete local criterion AG-CA-08, Theorem 4.2, to the actual local map of Noetherian rings $\widehat A\to\widehat B$ and the module $\widehat B$. This module is finite over the stipulated target $\widehat B$, which is the required finiteness condition; no finiteness over $\widehat A$ is being assumed. The vanishing just proved gives flatness.

Its closed fibre is nonzero: $\mathfrak m\widehat B\subset\mathfrak n\widehat B$, so $\widehat B/\mathfrak m\widehat B$ surjects onto the nonzero field $B/\mathfrak n$. The entire local faithful-flatness proof AG-CA-08, Theorem 2.1, therefore makes the map faithfully flat. This proves the full assertion without identifying the two residue fields. ∎

Lemma F.100: check G ring maximal ideals

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 13001–13037.

A Noetherian ring $R$ is a G-ring if and only if $R_{\mathfrak m}$ has geometrically regular formal fibres for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.

Proof. If $R$ is a G-ring, definition F.92 gives the stated property at every maximal ideal. Conversely assume those properties, and fix any prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$. Choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supset\mathfrak p$. Put $C=\widehat{R_{\mathfrak m}}$. The local completion map $R_{\mathfrak m}\to C$ is faithfully flat by AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.2. Hence its fibre at $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak m}$ is nonzero. Choose a prime of that fibre and take its preimage $\mathfrak p'\subset C$; the residue-field map is injective, so its contraction is exactly $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak m}$. This is the prime lifting supplied by faithful flatness.

Set $B=C_{\mathfrak p'}$ and $\widehat B=\widehat{C_{\mathfrak p'}}$. The map $R_{\mathfrak p}\to B$ is local and flat: it is induced by the localized completion map, and its closed prime contraction is $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$. A local map sends every power of the source maximal ideal into the corresponding power of the target maximal ideal. Taking inverse limits therefore constructs the map $\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\to\widehat B$. Naturality of reduction makes both squares in the actual diagram commute: $$\begin{array}{ccccc} C&\longrightarrow&B&\longrightarrow&\widehat B\\ \uparrow&&\uparrow&&\uparrow\\ R_{\mathfrak m}&\longrightarrow&R_{\mathfrak p}&\longrightarrow&\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}. \end{array}$$

All rings here are Noetherian. By assumption and completion flatness, the first vertical map $R_{\mathfrak m}\to C$ is regular. The map $C\to B$ is regular: localization is flat; at a prime of $C$ its fibre is its residue field if the multiplicative set avoids that prime, and the zero ring otherwise. Every extension of that residue field leaves a field, hence a regular ring. Also $C$ is complete Noetherian local, so F.132 makes it a G-ring and gives regularity of $B\to\widehat B$. Applying F.124 twice proves $R_{\mathfrak m}\to\widehat B$ regular.

This composite factors through $R_{\mathfrak p}$. It makes $\widehat B$ flat over $R_{\mathfrak p}$: tensoring any injection of $R_{\mathfrak p}$-modules with $\widehat B$ is the same as tensoring the underlying $R_{\mathfrak m}$-modules, by the localization universal property. Its fibres at primes of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ are the corresponding fibres over $R_{\mathfrak m}$, since their residue fields are identical. Thus $R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat B$ is regular as well.

The proved flat local map $R_{\mathfrak p}\to B$ satisfies precisely the hypotheses of F.99A, which makes the induced map $\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\to\widehat B$ faithfully flat. The factorization in the right square and F.125 therefore descend regularity of $R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat B$ to regularity of $R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}$. As $\mathfrak p$ was arbitrary, F.92 says $R$ is a G-ring. For the zero ring both sets of tests are empty, so the equivalence still holds. ∎

Lemma F.101: conormal sequence H1 regular ideal

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07CX.

For ideals $I\subset J$ of an arbitrary ring $A$, suppose the ideal $J/I$ of $A/I$ is $H_1$-regular. Then $$ I\cap J^2=IJ. $$

Proof. The inclusion $IJ\subset I\cap J^2$ follows from $I\subset J$. We prove the other inclusion at each prime of $A$. Exact localization commutes with the intersection, the product and the quotient in this assertion; the fraction proof and the detection of a zero module are S01, Lemma 1.1. These facts will turn the local equalities into the global one.

At a prime outside $V(J)$, the ideal $J$ becomes the unit ideal, and both sides become $I$. At a prime containing $J$, localize $A$ there. The defining neighbourhood in F.95 supplies a finite list $g_1,\ldots,g_s\in J$ whose images generate $J/I$ and have zero first Koszul homology over $A/I$. Indeed we can lift the list from its quotient neighbourhood and localize further at the prime; exact localization preserves cycles, boundaries and their homology. In this local ring $J=I+(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$.

Take $x\in I\cap J^2$. Expanding a finite expression for $x$ as a sum of products of members of $J$ gives $$ x=u+\sum_{i=1}^s g_i b_i, \qquad u\in IJ,\quad b_i\in J. $$ Terms having a factor in $I$ were absorbed in $u$; all other terms have two factors from the displayed list. Reducing modulo $I$ makes $(\bar b_i)$ a degree-one Koszul cycle because its scalar product with $(\bar g_i)$ is zero. The zero first homology says this cycle is a boundary. With the convention $$ \partial(e_i\wedge e_j)=\bar g_i e_j-\bar g_j e_i, $$ it is a finite sum of these displayed vectors with coefficients in $A/I$.

Lift those coefficients to $A$ and subtract the corresponding vectors $g_i e_j-g_j e_i$ from $(b_i)$. Their scalar products with $(g_i)$ are exactly zero in $A$, so this subtraction leaves $\sum_i g_i b_i$ unchanged. Its new coefficients reduce to zero modulo $I$, hence belong to $I$. The sum is therefore in $IJ$, as is $u$, proving $x\in IJ$. An empty list gives the same calculation with sum zero. No finite generation of $I$ and no Noetherian condition were used. Applying local detection to $(I\cap J^2)/IJ$ completes the proof. ∎

Lemma F.102: cotangent complex symmetric algebra

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07EV.

Let $A$ be any ring and let $$ 0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow A^m\xrightarrow{q}M\longrightarrow0 $$ be exact, where $M$ is finite projective. Set $C=\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)$ and let $\alpha:A[y_1,\ldots,y_m]\twoheadrightarrow C$ be the presentation induced by $q$, with kernel $J$. The natural map $$ K\otimes_A C\longrightarrow J/J^2, \qquad (k_1,\ldots,k_m)\otimes c \longmapsto c\sum_i k_i y_i\bmod J^2 $$ is an isomorphism. With this identification the conormal complex and its cokernel are $$ \operatorname{NL}(\alpha)=[K\otimes_A C\longrightarrow C^m], \qquad \Omega_{C/A}=M\otimes_A C, $$ where the differential is obtained from $K\hookrightarrow A^m$ by tensoring with $C$.

Proof. Choose a section $s:M\to A^m$ using projectivity. The map $(k,m)\mapsto k+s(m)$ identifies $K\oplus M$ with $A^m$: its inverse sends $a$ to $(a-sq(a),q(a))$. We compute the presentation using this decomposition, keeping track of its specified natural map.

For a module $V$, the symmetric algebra is the tensor algebra modulo the relations that interchange two adjacent factors. A linear map $V\to D$ into a commutative $A$-algebra extends on a pure tensor by multiplying its images; the interchange relations vanish, and these products determine the extension uniquely. This proves the symmetric-algebra universal property from the tensor construction S01, Lemma 1.0. It also gives its grading by tensor degree, with degree zero $A$ and degree one $V$.

That property and the algebra tensor universal property give inverse maps $$ \operatorname{Sym}_A(K\oplus M) \ \cong\ \operatorname{Sym}_A(K)\otimes_A C. $$ In one direction send $k$ to $k\otimes1$ and $m$ to $1\otimes m$. In the other direction use the inclusions of $K$ and $M$ into $K\oplus M$ on the two tensor factors. Both composites fix the algebra generators, hence are identities. Likewise the symmetric algebra of $A^m$ is the polynomial ring on its coordinate basis. Under these identifications $\alpha$ is the augmentation on the $K$ factor and the identity on $C$.

Grade the tensor product by $K$ degree. The direct-sum tensor formula of S01, Lemma 1.0 gives $$ J=\bigoplus_{d\ge1}\operatorname{Sym}_A^d(K)\otimes_A C, \qquad J^2=\bigoplus_{d\ge2}\operatorname{Sym}_A^d(K)\otimes_A C. $$ For the second equality, a product of positive degrees has degree at least two. Conversely each degree-$d$ term is generated by products $k_1\cdots k_d\otimes c$; when $d\ge2$ separate its first factor from the rest to express it as a product of two elements of $J$. Quotienting thus leaves precisely $K\otimes_A C$. Its generator $k\otimes c$ corresponds in the original coordinates to $c\sum_i k_i y_i$, proving exactly the natural isomorphism in the statement, independently of the auxiliary section.

Relative differentiation sends this linear polynomial to $\sum_i k_i\,dy_i$. The polynomial differentials are free on these $m$ symbols, so the displayed complex has exactly the claimed differential. Tensoring the split sequence with $C$ remains split exact, and its cokernel is $M\otimes_A C$. This proves the assertion about $\Omega_{C/A}$ as well, including zero modules and the empty coordinate basis.

The projectivity hypothesis prevents additional conormal relations. For example let $A=k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$, let $M=k^2$ via $\varepsilon M=0$, and let $q:A^2\to M$ be reduction. Then $K=\varepsilon A^2$, $C=A[y_1,y_2]/(\varepsilon y_1,\varepsilon y_2)$, and $J=(\varepsilon y_1,\varepsilon y_2)$ has square zero. The source $K\otimes_A C$ is $k[y_1,y_2]^2$, whereas the vector $(y_2,-y_1)$ maps to $\varepsilon y_1y_2-\varepsilon y_2y_1=0$ in $J/J^2$ and is nonzero in that source. Thus the same conormal identity need not hold after dropping the hypothesis. ∎

Lemma F.103: degree p extension regular

Let $R$ be a Noetherian regular ring and let $D:R\to R$ be a derivation such that $D(f)$ is a unit. For every integer-coefficient polynomial $P(Z)$, the ring $R[Z]/(P(Z)-f)$ is regular. In particular this holds for $P(Z)=Z^n$, $n\ge1$, including degree-$p$ adjunctions in characteristic $p$.

The identity $D(1)=2D(1)$ gives $D(1)=0$; additivity and additive inverses then give $D(n)=0$ for every integer scalar $n$. Hence $D_V(P)=0$ and $$D_V(P-f)=-D(f).$$ This is a unit already in $V$, and remains a unit in its quotient. The entire hypersurface result F.122, with its localized-derivation and parameter-quotient proofs, applies to $V$ and $P-f$. It makes the quotient regular, for every specified $P$. Lemma F.104: derivation extends

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12363–12405.

Let $D:R\to R$ be a derivation of an arbitrary ring.

  1. It extends uniquely to every localization $U^{-1}R$.
  2. For every ideal $I$, it has a canonical continuous extension to $\widehat R=\varprojlim_n R/I^n$, with its inverse-limit topology. This extension is unique among continuous extensions.
  3. If $R\subset R'$ is finite type, $g\in R$ is a nonzerodivisor in $R'$, and the inclusions identify $R_g=R'_g$, then some $g^ND$ extends to a derivation $R'\to R'$.

Proof. For (1), the map $r\mapsto r+\epsilon D(r)$ into $(U^{-1}R)[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ is a ring map. Each $s\in U$ has image with inverse $$s^{-1}-\epsilon s^{-2}D(s).$$ Localization's universal property therefore extends the map. Its constant component is the structural map on the localized ring, so its second component is a derivation, with formula $$D_U(r/s)=D(r)/s-rD(s)/s^2.$$ This constructs a well-defined derivation even with zero divisors. Any extension must have that formula by differentiating $s\,s^{-1}=1$, proving uniqueness.

For (2), a product of $n+1$ ideal elements differentiates into $I^n$; finite sums and coefficient derivatives give $$D(I^{n+1})\subset I^n\qquad(n\ge1).$$ For a compatible family $a=(a_n)\in\widehat R$, choose $r\in R$ representing $a_{n+1}$ and define its derivative's $n$th coordinate as $D(r)\bmod I^n$. Replacing $r$ changes its derivative by an element of $I^n$, so this is well defined. Comparing representatives of $a_{n+2}$ and $a_{n+1}$ gives compatibility of these derivative coordinates. They therefore define $\widehat D(a)\in\widehat R$.

Represent $a,b$ modulo $I^{n+1}$ by $r,s$. Their sum and product are represented by $r+s,rs$. The identities in $R$, reduced modulo $I^n$, give $$ \widehat D(a+b)_n=\widehat D(a)_n+\widehat D(b)_n,\qquad \widehat D(ab)_n=a_n\widehat D(b)_n+b_n\widehat D(a)_n. $$ Thus the inverse-limit map is a derivation and extends $D$ through the canonical map $R\to\widehat R$.

Write $K_n=\ker(\widehat R\to R/I^n)$. The formula gives $\widehat D(K_{n+1})\subset K_n$, proving continuity. Canonical images of $R$ are dense: any coordinate modulo $I^m$ has a representative in $R$, matching all lower coordinates too. If another continuous extension were given, their difference would be a continuous additive map vanishing on this dense image. For a prescribed output coordinate choose a sufficiently deep input kernel mapped into its kernel by continuity, and choose an $R$-representative matching that input coordinate. The difference has zero prescribed output coordinate. This holds for every coordinate, and the inverse limit is separated, so the difference is zero. The construction uses the inverse-limit kernels, without assuming an infinitely generated ideal's extended powers agree with those kernels.

For (3), $R'$ embeds in $R'_g$: if $x/1=0$, some $g^j x=0$, and injectivity of multiplication by $g$ repeatedly gives $x=0$. Choose algebra generators $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ of $R'/R$. The localized equality writes each as a fraction from $R$ with denominator a power of $g$; the embedding just proved makes those cleared equalities hold in $R'$. Thus a common $n\ge0$ satisfies $g^nx_i\in R$ for every $i$.

Inside the common localization apply (1). The product rule, including $D(g^n)=ng^{n-1}D(g)$ when $n>0$, gives $$g^{n+1}D_U(x_i)=gD(g^nx_i)-n(g^nx_i)D(g)\in R.$$ For $n=0$ the second term is zero and the same identity holds directly. Multiplying a derivation by the scalar $g^{n+1}$ still gives a derivation. It sends $R$ into $R$ and each generator into $R$, so repeated product and sum rules send every polynomial expression in the generators into $R'$. Since this is the restriction of an actual derivation on the localization, all relations in $R'$ are respected. Restriction therefore gives the required extension with $N=n+1$. Empty generator lists and the zero ring cause no exception. ∎

Lemma F.105: find D

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12469–12520.

Let $p$ be prime, let $B$ be a domain of characteristic $p$, and let $f\in B$ be outside $\operatorname{Frac}(B)^p$. If $B$ is finite type over a complete Noetherian local ring, there is a derivation $D:B\to B$ with $D(f)\ne0$.

Proof. Let $R_1\to B$ be such a finite-type map. Its kernel is prime. Exact completion on finite modules AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.1 identifies the quotient $R_1/\ker(R_1\to B)$ with its maximal-adic completion: tensor the finite quotient with $\widehat{R_1}=R_1$. Thus its image is again a complete Noetherian local domain, of characteristic $p$. By F.25 it is finite over an embedded power-series ring $R=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$. A finite module generating list for the image ring, together with the finite algebra generating list for $B$ over that image, makes $B$ finite type over $R$. In particular $R\subset B$ is injective.

Put $K_0=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. Noether normalization AG-CA-09, Corollary 3.2 supplies algebraically independent parameters in $B\otimes_RK_0$ over which that algebra is finite. Multiply each parameter by a nonzero scalar of $R$ to put it in $B$; independence and the parameter algebra over $K_0$ are unchanged. Write the resulting parameters as $y_1,\ldots,y_d$, and put $A=R[y_1,\ldots,y_d]$. Choose finite $A$-algebra generators $b_i$ of $B$. Each satisfies a monic equation over $K_0[y]$. There is a common nonzero $g\in R$ for which every coefficient belongs to $A_g$.

Write such an equation as $b_i^{e_i}+\sum_{j<e_i}c_{ij}b_i^j=0$. Choose $N$ such that $g^{N(e_i-j)}c_{ij}\in A$ for every $i,j$. Multiplying by $g^{Ne_i}$ gives a monic equation over $A$ for $g^Nb_i$. Consequently $$B'=A[g^Nb_1,\ldots,g^Nb_t]\subset B$$ is finite over $A$: reduce powers of each generator using its monic equation, obtaining a finite spanning list of bounded monomials. Moreover $B'_g=B_g$, since all $b_i$ belong to $B'_g$. A sufficiently large $r\geq0$ therefore puts $f'=g^{pr}f$ in $B'$. The fraction fields of $B'$ and $B$ agree; call this field $L$. Since $g^{pr}=(g^r)^p$, membership of $f'$ in $L^p$ would imply membership of $f$ in $L^p$. Thus $f'\notin L^p$. Finiteness over $A$ makes $L$ finite over $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$: the localization $B'\otimes_AK$ is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field, and contains all fractions of $B'$.

The complete power-series calculation F.120 supplies a nonempty downward-directed family of coefficient subrings $$A_J=k_J[[X_1^p,\ldots,X_n^p]][y_1^p,\ldots,y_d^p]\subset A,$$ with $A$ finite free over $A_J$ and fraction fields $K_J$ containing $K^p$, whose intersection is $K^p$. Here $J$ runs over finite subsets of an absolute $p$-basis of $k$, and $k_J$ is generated over $k^p$ by the basis elements outside $J$; no perfection hypothesis is imposed. The finite-extension assertion of F.112 gives $\bigcap_JL^pK_J=L^p$. Since $f'\notin L^p$, choose $J$ with $f'\notin L^pK_J$.

The relative $p$-basis theorem F.119 extends $\{f'\}$ to a $p$-basis of $L/K_J$. Indeed its first degree is $p$: a proper monic factor of $T^p-(f')^p=(T-f')^p$ has coefficient $-ef'$, $1\leq e<p$, and would put $f'$ in $L^pK_J$. The coordinate derivation from the full presentation in F.119 consequently gives $\delta:L\to L$ killing $K_J$ with $\delta(f')=1$.

The ring $B'$ is finite over $A_J$, by the two finite module spanning lists. Choose $A_J$-module generators $v_1,\ldots,v_s$. Write each $\delta(v_i)$ as a fraction of $B'$ and let $h\in B'\setminus\{0\}$ be the product of their nonzero denominators. Then $D'=h\delta$ sends every $v_i$ into $B'$ and kills $A_J$. Differentiating an arbitrary expression $\sum_i a_iv_i$, $a_i\in A_J$, proves $D'(B')\subset B'$. Its value on $f'$ is $h\ne0$.

Finally $B$ is finite type over $B'$, $g$ is a nonzerodivisor in both domains, and $B'_g=B_g$. The third assertion of F.104 therefore gives $s\geq0$ for which $g^sD'$ restricts to a derivation $D:B\to B$. In the common fraction field, the fraction formula and $D'(g^{pr})=prg^{pr-1}D'(g)=0$ yield $$D(f)=g^sD'(g^{-pr}f')=g^{s-pr}h\ne0.$$ Its membership in $B$ follows from the restriction just proved; the displayed expression proves its nonvanishing. Empty parameter lists or a coefficient field as base require no changes. ∎

Lemma F.106: formally smooth

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07EC.

Let $\varphi:R\to S$ be continuous. If the underlying algebra map is formally smooth, it is formally smooth when $R$ has any linear topology and $S$ has a pre-adic topology. Moreover, if the topologies on $R$ and $S$ are given by the powers of ideals $\mathfrak m$ and $\mathfrak n$, formal smoothness is unchanged when the topology on $R$ is replaced by the discrete topology.

Proof. We specify the topological test. Give a ring $D$ and its quotient $D/J$ the discrete topology, where $J^2=0$. Fix continuous maps $a:R\to D$ and $b:S\to D/J$ such that $b\varphi$ is the reduction of $a$. A solution is a continuous $R$-algebra map $c:S\to D$ reducing to $b$. Topological formal smoothness requires a solution for every such test; algebraic formal smoothness uses the same tests without continuity conditions. The latter definition is AG-CA-17, Section 1.

For a pre-adic topology on $S$, choose $\mathfrak n$ whose powers form a neighbourhood basis at zero. A ring map from $S$ to a discrete ring is continuous precisely when its kernel contains some $\mathfrak n^r$: continuity at zero gives this condition, and translation gives continuity at every point. Algebraic formal smoothness supplies a lift $c$ in the test. Continuity of $b$ gives $b(\mathfrak n^r)=0$ for some $r\ge1$. Thus $c(\mathfrak n^r)\subset J$, and multiplication of two such ideal powers gives $$ c(\mathfrak n^{2r})\subset J^2=0. $$ The lift is therefore continuous. The linear topology on $R$ needs no further restriction beyond continuity of the stipulated maps.

Now assume both topologies are given by the stated ideal powers. If formal smoothness holds with discrete $R$, any test with continuous $a$ is among its tests, so the same property holds with the original topology on $R$. In the other direction, start with a test having discrete $R$; the map $a$ is initially allowed to be arbitrary. Continuity of $\varphi$ gives an integer $s\ge1$ with $\varphi(\mathfrak m^s)\subset\mathfrak n$. For the integer $r$ supplied by $b$ as above, compatibility implies $$ a(\mathfrak m^{sr})\subset J, \qquad a(\mathfrak m^{2sr})=0. $$ Hence $a$ was continuous for the $\mathfrak m$-power topology as well. Formal smoothness for that topology now gives the desired continuous lift. This proves both directions, with no finite-generation or Noetherian assumption. Neither completeness nor separatedness of $S$ was required. ∎

Lemma F.107: formally smooth completion

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07ED.

Let $R\to S$ be a continuous map of Noetherian rings with topologies defined by finitely generated ideals $\mathfrak m\subset R$ and $\mathfrak n\subset S$. Write $\widehat R$ and $\widehat S$ for the corresponding completions. The following three properties are equivalent: $R\to S$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak n$-power topology; $R\to\widehat S$ is formally smooth for the $\mathfrak n\widehat S$-power topology; and $\widehat R\to\widehat S$ is formally smooth for that target topology.

Proof. The continuous map induces the last completion map by applying it to compatible finite-order coordinates. AG-CA-19, Proposition 2.2 proves the exact quotient identities $$ \widehat R/\mathfrak m^q\widehat R=R/\mathfrak m^q, \qquad \widehat S/\mathfrak n^q\widehat S=S/\mathfrak n^q \quad(q\ge1). $$ These identities use the canonical maps and commute with all transition maps. That proposition also proves completeness for the extended-ideal topologies.

A continuous homomorphism $u:S\to D$ to a discrete ring kills some $\mathfrak n^q$. Its factorization through $S/\mathfrak n^q$ and the second displayed identity define a homomorphism $\widehat u:\widehat S\to D$ killing $\mathfrak n^q\widehat S$. It extends $u$. It is the only continuous extension: any other extension kills a possibly different ideal power; pass to an exponent at least as large as both, where its map is determined by the same surjective finite quotient. Restriction and extension are inverse, and they commute with maps between discrete target rings. The identical argument applies to $R$ and $\widehat R$.

Use the tests defined in F.106, with $D\to D/J$ square-zero. First compare $R\to S$ with $R\to\widehat S$. Keep the structural map from $R$ fixed. The just-proved correspondence identifies every continuous map to $D/J$, every continuous lift to $D$, and their compatibility with $R$. Thus one test has a solution exactly when its counterpart does.

Next compare $R\to\widehat S$ with $\widehat R\to\widehat S$. With the original topology on the base, extension and restriction identify the structural maps to both discrete test rings. Compatibility after restriction implies compatibility after extension: the two continuous maps from $\widehat R$ agree by uniqueness of extension. The test diagrams and their dotted lifts therefore correspond in both directions. Finally F.106 identifies each of these topological-base tests with the tests using discrete base. In particular a structural map allowed in a discrete-base test is automatically continuous when it is compatible with the continuous target map modulo $J$; that is precisely the ideal-power calculation in F.106. This proves the three equivalences in the stipulated Noetherian scope. ∎

Lemma F.108: gamma commutative diagram

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07E3.

Consider a commutative square of fields with arrows $k\to k'$, $k\to K$, $k'\to K'$ and $K\to K'$. Assume $k'/k$ and $K'/K$ are finitely generated. For the natural maps $$ \alpha:\Omega_{K/k}\otimes_KK'\longrightarrow\Omega_{K'/k'}, \qquad \beta:H_1(L_{K/k})\otimes_KK'\longrightarrow H_1(L_{K'/k'}), $$ all four kernels and cokernels are finite-dimensional, and $$ \dim\ker\alpha-\dim\operatorname{coker}\alpha -\dim\ker\beta+\dim\operatorname{coker}\beta =\operatorname{trdeg}_k k'-\operatorname{trdeg}_K K'. $$

Proof. All vector spaces below are over $K'$, and all omitted scalar extensions are to $K'$. Apply the full field-transitivity proof F.131 to $k\subset k'\subset K'$ and $k\subset K\subset K'$. Let $$ V=H_1(L_{K'/k}),\qquad U=\Omega_{K'/k}. $$ For the first row put $P_1=H_1(L_{k'/k})\otimes_{k'}K'$, $W_1=H_1(L_{K'/k'})$, $Q_1=\Omega_{k'/k}\otimes_{k'}K'$ and $Z_1=\Omega_{K'/k'}$. For the second put $P_2=H_1(L_{K/k})\otimes_KK'$, $W_2=H_1(L_{K'/K})$, $Q_2=\Omega_{K/k}\otimes_KK'$ and $Z_2=\Omega_{K'/K}$. The two exact rows are $$ 0\longrightarrow P_i\longrightarrow V\longrightarrow W_i \longrightarrow Q_i\longrightarrow U\longrightarrow Z_i\longrightarrow0 \qquad(i=1,2). $$ Their first injections identify $P_1,P_2$ with subspaces of $V$. Naturality of the representative and derivative maps in F.42 identifies $\beta$ with $P_2\to V\to W_1$ and $\alpha$ with $Q_2\to U\to Z_1$.

We calculate only finite defects, so no subtraction of infinite dimensions is involved. Set $$ T=P_1\cap P_2,\quad Y=V/(P_1+P_2),\quad A_i=\ker(Q_i\to U),\quad B_i=\operatorname{im}(Q_i\to U). $$ Write $i_0=\dim T$, $r=\dim(P_1/T)$, $y=\dim Y$, $a_i=\dim A_i$, $j=\dim(B_1\cap B_2)$, $s=\dim(B_1/(B_1\cap B_2))$ and $z=\dim(U/(B_1+B_2))$. These are finite. Indeed F.98 makes $P_1,Q_1,W_2,Z_2$ finite. The space $Y$ is a quotient of $V/P_2$, which embeds in $W_2$; $A_2$ is a quotient of $W_2$; and the space measured by $z$ is a quotient of $Z_2$. All other spaces on the list are subspaces or quotients of $P_1$ or $Q_1$.

The kernel of $\beta$ is $T$. Exactness of the first row gives an injection $V/P_1\to W_1$ with quotient $A_1$. Dividing its image by the image of $P_2$ therefore yields $$ 0\longrightarrow Y\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}\beta \longrightarrow A_1\longrightarrow0. $$ For $\alpha$, its kernel consists of the elements of $Q_2$ whose image in $U$ lies in $B_1$. Mapping them into $U$ gives a surjection onto $B_1\cap B_2$ with kernel $A_2$. Its cokernel is $U/(B_1+B_2)$. Hence $$ \dim\ker\beta=i_0,\quad \dim\operatorname{coker}\beta=y+a_1, \qquad \dim\ker\alpha=a_2+j,\quad \dim\operatorname{coker}\alpha=z. $$ The second row identifies $V/P_2$ with the kernel of $W_2\to Q_2$. Inside $V/P_2$, the image of $P_1$ is $P_1/T$ and has quotient $Y$. Similarly $U/B_2$ contains the image $B_1/(B_1\cap B_2)$ with quotient $U/(B_1+B_2)$. The resulting finite exact sequences give $$ \dim P_1=i_0+r,\quad \dim W_2=r+y+a_2, \qquad \dim Q_1=a_1+j+s,\quad \dim Z_2=s+z. $$ Subtracting these finite numbers shows that the expression in the statement equals $$ (a_2+j)-z-i_0+(y+a_1) =\dim Q_1-\dim P_1-\dim Z_2+\dim W_2. $$ F.98 applied to $k'/k$ and $K'/K$ gives the required transcendence-degree difference. This also proves finiteness of every defect without requiring $K/k$ or $K'/k'$ to be finitely generated. ∎

Lemma F.109: geometrically regular over field

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 9460–9501.

Let $k$ have characteristic $p>0$, and let $(A,\mathfrak m,K)$ be a geometrically regular Noetherian local $k$-algebra. Let $k\subset F\subset K$ be finitely generated over $k$. Suppose a map $\varphi:k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]\to A$ has residue images $\overline y_i\in F$, with $d\overline y_1,\ldots,d\overline y_m$ a basis of $\Omega_{F/k}$. Put $\mathfrak p=\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak m)$. Then $$k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]_{\mathfrak p}\longrightarrow A$$ is flat, and $A/\mathfrak pA$ is regular.

Proof. Write $R_0=k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]_{\mathfrak p}$, $\mathfrak m_0=\mathfrak pR_0$, and $K_0=R_0/\mathfrak m_0$. The residue map embeds $K_0$ into $F$, and $$K_0=k(\overline y_1,\ldots,\overline y_m).$$ Indeed it is the fraction field of the domain image of $k[y]$ in $K$; localizing at the kernel inverts every nonzero image. The polynomial and fraction differential formulas in AG-CA-15, Sections 1–2 and Theorem 5.1 make $\Omega_{R_0/k}$ free on $dy_i$, and make their images span $\Omega_{K_0/k}$. They are independent in that last space: a $K_0$-linear relation maps to an $F$-linear relation between the assumed basis of $\Omega_{F/k}$, so every coefficient vanishes in $F$, and hence in $K_0$. Thus $$\Omega_{R_0/k}\otimes_{R_0}K_0\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Omega_{K_0/k}.$$

The ring $R_0$ is regular local by iterating AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3 from the field and using the definition of a regular ring at its prime localizations. For a finite purely inseparable $k'/k$, its tensor is the localization of $k'[y]$ at the images of $k[y]\setminus\mathfrak p$, and is Noetherian regular. Criterion F.50 therefore makes $R_0$ geometrically regular over $k$. The geometric-regularity characterization F.133 gives injectivity of the connecting map $$\gamma_0:H_1(L_{K_0/k})\longrightarrow\mathfrak m_0/\mathfrak m_0^2.$$ The full quotient sequence F.42 gives $$H_1(L_{K_0/k})\longrightarrow\mathfrak m_0/\mathfrak m_0^2 \longrightarrow\Omega_{R_0/k}\otimes_{R_0}K_0 \longrightarrow\Omega_{K_0/k}\longrightarrow0.$$ The last nonzero arrow is the displayed isomorphism, so exactness also makes $\gamma_0$ surjective. Hence it is an isomorphism.

All arrows in the following square are the connecting and scalar-extension maps of the same quotient presentations: $$\begin{array}{ccc} H_1(L_{K_0/k})\otimes_{K_0}K&\xrightarrow{\gamma_0\otimes1}& (\mathfrak m_0/\mathfrak m_0^2)\otimes_{K_0}K\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ H_1(L_{K/k})&\xrightarrow{\gamma}&\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2. \end{array}$$ It commutes: a lifted polynomial relation has the same differentiated representative whether mapped first to $A$ or first to its residue field, as in F.42. The left arrow is injective by the first injection of the field-tower sequence F.131 for $k\subset K_0\subset K$. The bottom arrow is injective by F.133 applied to the assumed geometrically regular $A$. The top arrow is an isomorphism, since tensor over a field is exact. If a vector in its upper-right space maps to zero below, take its preimage in the upper-left space. Commutativity and the two injections force that preimage, and then the vector, to be zero. This proves injectivity of the right arrow.

Choose a regular system of parameters $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ of $R_0$. Their classes are a $K_0$-basis of $\mathfrak m_0/\mathfrak m_0^2$; after scalar extension they remain a $K$-basis. The right injection says their images have independent classes in $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. The ring $A$ is regular, by F.133. Extend those classes to a basis of this finite-dimensional $K$-space and lift the additional basis vectors to $\mathfrak m$. Nakayama's lemma F.10 makes the resulting list a minimal generating list for $\mathfrak m$. The complete parameter theorem AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1 makes it a regular sequence. In particular its prefix, the images of $x_1,\ldots,x_d$, is regular in $A$, with proper generated ideal.

The map $R_0\to A$ is local by the definition of $\mathfrak p$. Therefore F.46 applies to these images and proves flatness. The full successive parameter-quotient result AG-CA-14, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 makes $A/(x_1,\ldots,x_d)A$ regular local. Since the parameters generate $\mathfrak m_0$, their image ideal is exactly $\mathfrak pA$. This is the asserted regular quotient. If $d=0$, $R_0$ is a field, its flatness assertion is the vector-space argument, and the quotient is $A$ itself; the proof also covers $m=0$. ∎

Lemma F.110: helper G ring

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12915–12963.

Let $A_0$ be a regular complete Noetherian local domain, put $P=A_0[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]$, and let $\mathfrak q\subset P$ be any prime. Both $$\widehat{P_{\mathfrak q}}\otimes_{A_0}\operatorname{Frac}(A_0) \quad\hbox{and}\quad \widehat{P_{\mathfrak q}}\otimes_P\operatorname{Frac}(P)$$ are geometrically regular over their displayed fields. The second assertion contains the power-series helper; the first is the additional form used in F.97.

Proof. Polynomial regularity and localization are AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3 and Theorem 3.2. Thus $P_{\mathfrak q}$ is regular local. Its completion $H=\widehat{P_{\mathfrak q}}$ is Noetherian regular local by AG-CA-19, Theorem 4.1. Each displayed ring is a localization of $H$, so is Noetherian and regular. If the indicated field has characteristic zero, its only finite purely inseparable extension is itself, and F.50 proves geometric regularity.

Suppose the characteristic is $p>0$. In this case $A_0\cong k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$, with no assumption that $k$ is perfect. To check this specialization, AG-CA-19S, Theorem 6.1 evaluates the variables at a minimal list of generators of the maximal ideal of $A_0$, giving a surjection from $k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$. Regularity makes $n=\dim A_0$. The source is regular local of dimension $n$, by the polynomial completion calculation and AG-CA-19, Theorem 4.1. If the kernel contained a nonzero element, the one-equation dimension theorem AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.2 would make the quotient dimension at most $n-1$, a contradiction. The evaluation kernel is therefore zero.

Treat the two assertions together by taking $Q=A_0$, $F=\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)$ in the first case, and $Q=P$, $F=\operatorname{Frac}(P)$ in the second. We prove that $H\otimes_Q L$ is regular for every finite purely inseparable extension $L/F$, by induction on its degree. The base case is the localization already proved regular. Such an extension has a tower of degree-$p$ steps: take finite field generators, with successive $p$-powers in $F$, and adjoin their roots one at a time; at a nontrivial step the proper-factor argument in F.119 gives degree $p$. Thus at the final step write $F\subset M\subset L=M(z)$, $z^p=f\in M\setminus M^p$, and assume $E=H\otimes_QM$ regular.

There is a finite domain $B$, $Q\subset B\subset M$, with fraction field $M$ and, after rescaling $z$, with $f\in B$. Here are the denominator details. Choose finitely many algebraic generators $u_i$ of $M/F$. For a monic equation $u_i^{d_i}+\sum_{j<d_i}c_{ij}u_i^j=0$, multiplication by a suitable nonzero $a_i\in Q$ makes every $a_i^{d_i-j}c_{ij}$ lie in $Q$. Hence $a_iu_i$ is integral over $Q$. The algebra generated by these elements is finite by bounded monic reductions, and its fraction field is $M$. Write $f=b/d$ in that algebra. A monic integral equation for $d\ne0$ can be shortened, by cancelling powers of $d$ in this domain, until its constant coefficient $a\in Q$ is nonzero. The equation expresses $a/d$ in $B$. Replace $z$ by $az$. Its new $p$th power is $a^pf=b a^{p-1}(a/d)\in B$, and remains outside $M^p$, since $a^p$ is a nonzero $p$th power. Relabel this generator and its power as $z,f$. The monic irreducible equation makes $C=B[Z]/(Z^p-f)$ a finite domain with fraction field $L$; injectivity in $L$ follows from the degree-$p$ minimal polynomial.

The base $Q$ is a normal domain. In the first case this is regular local normality; in the second it is polynomial regularity followed by AG-CA-15, Corollary 4.5. Every element of $B$ or $C$ has some $p$-power in $F$, since its fraction field is finite purely inseparable over $F$. That power is integral over $Q$, because the element is integral. Normality therefore puts the power in $Q$.

Set $T=B[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]$ in the first case, and $T=B$ in the second. Then $P\subset T$ is finite, and every element of $T$ has a sufficiently high $p$-power in $P$. For a polynomial in the first case, take a common exponent for its finitely many coefficients and apply Frobenius to the sum. Lying over gives a prime $\mathfrak r$ above $\mathfrak q$, and it is unique: for $t^{p^e}\in P$, membership of $t$ in a prime above $\mathfrak q$ is equivalent to membership of $t^{p^e}$ in $\mathfrak q$. The full finite-completion product theorem F.27 thus has one factor and gives $$H\otimes_PT\cong\widehat{T_{\mathfrak r}}.$$ Tensoring with $M=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ over $B$, and using $P\otimes_{A_0}B=T$ in the first case, gives the actual identity $$E=H\otimes_QM\cong\widehat{T_{\mathfrak r}}\otimes_BM.$$ In particular $E$ is a localization of a Noetherian completed local ring. These are the maximal-ideal completions specified in F.27, not a replacement by an unrelated topology.

The domain $B$ is finite type over the complete local ring $A_0$, in either case. Since $f\notin M^p$, F.105 produces a derivation $D:B\to B$ with $D(f)\ne0$. Extend it coefficientwise to $T$ in the first case, assigning zero to the $Y_i$; coefficient convolution proves the product rule. In the second case it is already a derivation of $T$. By F.104 it extends successively to $T_{\mathfrak r}$, its maximal-adic completion, and the localization by $B\setminus\{0\}$. The resulting derivation of $E$ sends $f$ to the original nonzero element $D(f)\in M$. This is a unit in every nonzero $M$-algebra $E$; if $E=0$, the next test ring is also zero and already regular.

Finally tensor associativity and $L=M[Z]/(Z^p-f)$ give $$H\otimes_QL\cong E\otimes_ML\cong E[Z]/(Z^p-f).$$ The polynomial quotient identity follows by reducing each polynomial to its degree-less-than-$p$ remainder, or directly from its finite monic presentation. F.103 applies: $E$ is Noetherian regular and its derivation has unit value on $f$. It proves this next ring regular. The induction covers every finite purely inseparable extension. Criterion F.50 now gives both assertions. Empty lists of $X_i$ or $Y_i$ are included throughout. ∎

Lemma F.111: helper integral

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 09XG.

Let \(A\to B\) be an integral ring map, \(I\subset A\) an ideal, and \(y\in B\) have idempotent image in \(B/IB\). There are an integer \(d\geq1\) and a monic polynomial \(f(T)\in A[T]\) such that \[ f(y)=0,\qquad f(T)\bmod I=T^d(T-1)^d. \]

Proof. Write \(z=y^2-y=\sum_{i=1}^h a_ib_i\) with \(a_i\in I\) and \(b_i\in B\). This is a finite sum by the definition of the extended ideal. The subalgebra \(C=A[y,b_1,\ldots,b_h]\subset B\) is a finite \(A\)-module: each of its finitely many generators satisfies a monic equation over \(A\), and successive substitution reduces every monomial to one whose exponent in each generator is below that equation's degree. Those finitely many bounded monomials generate \(C\). This argument uses the image of \(A\); injectivity of \(A\to B\) is unnecessary.

Choose a finite module generating list \(c_1,\ldots,c_d\) for \(C\), including \(1\), so \(d\geq1\). Since \(zC\subset IC\), express each \(zc_i\) as \(\sum_j m_{ij}c_j\) with all \(m_{ij}\in I\). For the column \(c=(c_i)\) these equations say \((z1_d-M)c=0\), where \(M=(m_{ij})\). Multiplying by the adjugate, whose identity was proved completely in F.19, gives \[ g(z)c_i=0\quad\hbox{for all }i, \qquad g(U)=\det(U1_d-M)\in A[U]. \] The included generator \(1\) makes \(g(z)=0\) in \(C\), hence in \(B\). The determinant expansion makes \(g\) monic of degree \(d\); reducing the entries of \(M\) modulo \(I\) gives \(g(U)\bmod I=U^d\). Set \(f(T)=g(T^2-T)\). Its leading coefficient is \(1\), it annihilates \(y\), and its reduction is \((T^2-T)^d=T^d(T-1)^d\). The same construction permits an empty sum for \(z\), the zero target algebra, and \(I=A\). ∎

Lemma F.112: intersection subfields

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12067–12128.

Let $K$ have characteristic $p>0$. Let $(F_\lambda)$ be a nonempty downward-directed family of subfields of $K$ containing $K^p$, with intersection $K^p$. Then $$ \bigcap_\lambda\ker\bigl(\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}\to\Omega_{K/F_\lambda}\bigr)=0. $$ For every finite field extension $L/K$, the composita in $L$ also satisfy $$\bigcap_\lambda L^pF_\lambda=L^p.$$

Proof. Take an absolute $p$-basis of $K$ by the entire F.119. If a nonzero absolute differential $\omega$ vanished in every indicated relative module, write it in that differential basis using a finite nonempty subset $b_1,\ldots,b_c$ and coefficients not all zero. At every $\lambda$ those relative differentials would be dependent. F.119's full equivalence makes their $p$-monomials dependent over $F_\lambda K^p=F_\lambda$.

Index those finitely many monomials by $e$, $0\le e_i<p$, and form the actual $K$-subspace $$V=\{(a_e)\in K^{p^c}:\ \sum_e a_e b^e=0\}.$$ Its intersection with $F_\lambda^{p^c}$ is nonzero at every index. The entire newly proved F.113 gives a nonzero intersection with $(K^p)^{p^c}$, contradicting independence of the absolute $p$-basis monomials. Hence no such $\omega$ exists, proving the first assertion.

We prove the second assertion through finite simple steps. Here is the reduction for an arbitrary finite extension. Choose finitely many field generators $\alpha_i$. For each monic irreducible polynomial over $K$, remove a common factor $p$ from its positive exponents repeatedly until writing it as $G_i(T^{p^{e_i}})$ with $G_i'\ne0$. This terminates because its degree decreases. The polynomial $G_i$ is irreducible, since a factorization would give one of the original polynomial, and its nonzero derivative is relatively prime to it. Thus $\beta_i=\alpha_i^{p^{e_i}}$ is separable over $K$.

The field $M=K(\beta_i)$ is finite separable: at each successive adjunction its minimal polynomial divides the original squarefree polynomial over the larger coefficient field, and remains separable. The full separable-tower transitivity proof AG-CA-17, Lemma 7.1 proves that this tower is separable over $K$. From $M$, adjoin each successive $p$th root needed to recover the $\alpha_i$. Each step has degree one or $p$: if the root is absent, the proper-factor coefficient calculation in F.119 proves its degree-$p$ polynomial irreducible. This gives a tower of separable simple steps followed by degree-$p$ purely inseparable steps.

If the desired intersection identity has been proved up to an intermediate field $M$, the fields $E_\lambda=M^pF_\lambda\subset M$ are downward directed, contain $M^p$, and have intersection $M^p$. For the next field $N$, one has $N^pE_\lambda=N^pF_\lambda$, since $M^p\subset N^p$. Thus the same statement for that next simple step proves it for the composite. It remains to prove the two types of simple steps.

For a separable simple extension $L=K(\alpha)$, put $\theta=\alpha^p$. The minimal polynomial over $K(\alpha^p)$ divides both the original squarefree polynomial and $T^p-\alpha^p=(T-\alpha)^p$. It must therefore have degree one, so $K(\theta)=L$ and $\theta\in L^p$. Write $d=[L:K]$. Frobenius transports the $K$-basis $1,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha^{d-1}$ to the $K^p$-basis $1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{d-1}$ of $L^p$: raising expansions to the $p$th power proves spanning, and unique roots of coefficients prove independence. The same powers are a $K$-basis of $L$, because $K(\theta)=L$.

Consequently they are independent over every $F_\lambda\subset K$. Their monic relation over $K^p$ gives spanning over $F_\lambda$, so the algebra $F_\lambda[\theta]$ is a finite-dimensional domain and therefore a field, by multiplication and inversion. It is exactly $L^pF_\lambda$, with the displayed basis. An element in every compositum has a unique expansion in the $K$-basis of $L$; its coefficients must belong to every $F_\lambda$, hence to $K^p$. It therefore lies in $L^p$, proving the identity for this step.

For a nontrivial degree-$p$ purely inseparable step, write $L=K(\theta)$ with $\theta^p=t\in K\setminus K^p$. Frobenius of its power basis gives $$L^p=K^p(t),\qquad 1,t,\ldots,t^{p-1}\ \text{a }K^p\text{-basis}.$$ Choose $\lambda_0$ with $t\notin F_{\lambda_0}$, possible from the intersection assumption. Restrict to members contained in $F_{\lambda_0}$. This family is cofinal under refinement: downward directedness refines any given member together with $\lambda_0$. Its intersection is still $K^p$, by the same refinement argument in F.113, and taking the intersection of the composita over it does not change the full intersection.

For every such member, $t^p\in K^p\subset F_\lambda$ while $t\notin F_\lambda$. The proper-factor calculation gives degree $p$, so $L^pF_\lambda=F_\lambda(t)$ has basis $1,t,\ldots,t^{p-1}$. Use the unique expansion over the fixed coarse field $F_{\lambda_0}$; every refined-field expansion must have those same coefficients. They belong to all refined fields and hence to $K^p$. The element is therefore in $K^p(t)=L^p$. The reverse inclusion is automatic. This cofinal argument includes indices where $t$ was initially already in the field, without presuming a degree-$p$ basis there.

Both step types are proved. Applying the tower reduction establishes the identity for every finite extension, including the trivial one. Both assertions and all directed-family hypotheses have now been checked. ∎

Lemma F.113: intersection subfields subspace

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12027–12065.

Let $(F_\lambda)$ be a nonempty downward-directed family of subfields of a field $K$, and put $F=\bigcap_\lambda F_\lambda$. For every $K$-linear subspace $V\subset K^n$, $$ V\cap F^n\ne0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V\cap F_\lambda^n\ne0\ \text{for every }\lambda. $$

Proof. A nonzero vector in the intersection over $F$ belongs to every larger field's intersection. For the other implication induct on $n$. At $n=0$ both nonzero-intersection assertions are false, since the family is nonempty. At $n=1$, a $K$-subspace of $K$ is zero or all of $K$; the hypothesis excludes zero, and the vector one lies in $F$.

For $n>1$, let $V_0$ be the subspace of vectors of $V$ with first coordinate zero, viewed in $K^{n-1}$. If $V_0\cap F^{n-1}$ is nonzero, adjoining the zero first coordinate finishes the proof. Otherwise the induction hypothesis gives an index $\lambda_0$ with $V_0\cap F_{\lambda_0}^{n-1}=0$. Choose a nonzero vector of $V\cap F_{\lambda_0}^n$. Its first coordinate cannot vanish; divide by it to get a vector $v$ with first coordinate one.

For any other vector $w$ in this intersection, subtract $w_1v$. The difference is in $V_0\cap F_{\lambda_0}^{n-1}$ and hence zero. Thus its normalized vector is uniquely $v$. In particular, for every member $F_\mu\subset F_{\lambda_0}$, the hypothesized nonzero intersection contains a vector whose first coordinate is nonzero, and normalization gives this same $v$. All coordinates of $v$ consequently belong to the intersection of these refined fields.

That intersection is $F$. One inclusion follows because $F$ lies in every member. For the other, given any index $\lambda$, downward directedness supplies a member contained in both $F_{\lambda_0}$ and $F_\lambda$; membership in every refinement then implies membership in $F_\lambda$. Thus $v\in F^n$, and it is nonzero because its first coordinate is one. This proves the induction and the full equivalence. ∎

Lemma F.114: lci local

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07D1.

Let $R$ be Noetherian and let $S$ be a finitely presented $R$-algebra. A kernel of a finite polynomial presentation of $S$ is a regular ideal if and only if this property holds for polynomial presentations on a finite principal cover of $\operatorname{Spec}S$. The condition does not depend on the chosen presentations.

Proof. The arbitrary-ring comparison F.94.A proves presentation independence for Koszul-regular kernels. The finite polynomial rings and their localizations are Noetherian by AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1; its Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 1.2 make their finite-module submodules finite. In these rings, F.118 converts a Koszul-regular generating list in a local maximal ideal into a regular list. To obtain the neighbourhood condition in F.95, we will explicitly spread the successive injections, rather than infer global regularity merely from Koszul acyclicity.

Fix $P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\twoheadrightarrow S$ with kernel $I$, and a prime $\mathfrak q\supset I$ of $P$. Suppose a chart $S_g$ containing its image has a regular presentation. Choose $u\in P$ lifting $g$, so $u\notin\mathfrak q$. A presentation of that chart is $$ Q=P[Z]\twoheadrightarrow S_g,\qquad H=(I,t),\quad t=uZ-1. $$ The prime $\mathfrak q'$ of $Q$ given by $\mathfrak q$ and $Z=1/u$ satisfies $$ Q_{\mathfrak q'}/(t)=P_{\mathfrak q}. $$ Indeed quotienting first gives $P_u$, and then localization at the prime over $\mathfrak q$ gives $P_{\mathfrak q}$. Presentation comparison and F.118 give a regular generating list for $H_{\mathfrak q'}$. Its conormal classes are a basis by F.74. Meanwhile F.72 gives, at this point, $$ (H/H^2)_{\mathfrak q'} \cong (I/I^2)_{\mathfrak q}\oplus S_{\mathfrak q/I}\,t. $$ The first summand is a finite direct summand of a finite free module. It is flat and finitely presented, hence free over the local quotient by S01, Lemma 1.2. Choose $f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I$ whose classes are a basis there; denominators may be cleared since their values outside $\mathfrak q$ are units. The list $t,f_1,\ldots,f_c$ is a conormal basis. Nakayama applied to $H_{\mathfrak q'}/(t,f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ makes it a generator list for $H_{\mathfrak q'}$.

Compare it with the regular generator list just obtained. Both have the same length, equal to the conormal rank. Express the new list in the old one. Modulo the maximal ideal the coefficient matrix takes one basis of the conormal fibre to the other, so its determinant is a unit in $Q_{\mathfrak q'}$. Its exterior powers identify the Koszul complexes: the differential on a wedge deletes one entry with its alternating sign, and this formula commutes with the change of basis. Thus $t,f_1,\ldots,f_c$ has zero first homology. F.118 makes this very order regular, with $t$ first. Quotienting by $t$ proves that $f_1,\ldots,f_c$ is a regular list generating $I_{\mathfrak q}$.

Here is the required principal neighbourhood. The module $I/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$ is finite and vanishes at $\mathfrak q$. For each $i$, the kernel of multiplication by $f_i$ on $P/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})$ is also finite, because $P$ is Noetherian; it vanishes at $\mathfrak q$ by the just-proved regularity. Exact localization and the finite-generator fraction-zero argument S01, Lemma 1.1 give one element $h\notin\mathfrak q$ annihilating all these finitely many modules. In $P_h$ the list therefore generates $I_h$ and every successive multiplication is injective. Its final quotient is nonzero because the prime $\mathfrak qP_h$ still contains $I_h$. The list is regular on this actual neighbourhood, as required by F.95.

The argument applies at every point lying in one of the stipulated charts, hence at every prime above $I$. Conversely, localization preserves the successive injections of a regular list. For a chart where a given neighbourhood also inverts $u$, present the localization by adjoining $Z$ and put $uZ-1$ first. Multiplication by this polynomial is injective by its lowest-coefficient calculation, and its quotient is $P_u$; the remaining localized list is regular wherever the quotient is nonzero. Charts with zero quotient have no primes to check. Thus the kernel condition restricts to every principal chart. The local neighbourhoods cover the target, and a finite subcover exists by the finite unit-ideal calculation AG-CA-01, Proposition 2.3. Applying the same comparison to a second initial presentation proves the claimed independence. If $S=0$, all these prime conditions are vacuous, including the empty-cover case. ∎

Lemma F.115: lift factorization monic

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 0ALH.

Let $I\subset A$ be any ideal. Suppose the reduction of a monic $f\in A[T]$ has a factorization $\bar f=\bar G\bar H$ into coprime monic polynomials over $A/I$. There is a finitely presented étale map $A\to A'$ such that its canonical map $A/I\to A'/IA'$ is an isomorphism and $f=G'H'$ in $A'[T]$, with monic factors reducing to the prescribed ones.

Proof. If $I=A$, take $A'=0$, the principal localization at zero; its closed fibre and the prescribed factors are zero, so all requirements hold. Assume $A/I\ne0$. Put $d=\deg\bar G$ and $e=\deg\bar H$. Introduce $d+e$ variables for the lower coefficients of monic polynomials $G$ and $H$ of those degrees. The $d+e$ lower coefficients of $GH-f$ are equations in these variables. Write $C_0$ for their quotient algebra and $\Delta$ for the determinant of their square Jacobian matrix.

Over $D=A/I$, the derivative of multiplication at the given factors is $$ D[T]_{<d}\oplus D[T]_{<e}\longrightarrow D[T]_{<d+e}, \qquad (v,w)\longmapsto\bar H v+\bar G w. $$ Here $D[T]_{<r}$ is the free module on $1,T,\ldots,T^{r-1}$. Monic division works over this arbitrary ring: for a monic polynomial $p$ of degree $r$, subtract the current leading coefficient times $T^k p$ until the remainder has degree below $r$. For a nonzero polynomial $q$, the product $qp$ has degree $\deg q+r$, with the same nonzero leading coefficient as $q$. Hence no nonzero multiple of $p$ has degree below $r$, and the quotient and remainder are unique. For $r=0$, the monic polynomial is $1$ and the remainder is zero. Choose a Bezout identity $a\bar G+b\bar H=1$. For a polynomial $q$ in the right module, let $v$ be the remainder of $bq$ on monic division by $\bar G$. Then $q-\bar H v$ is divisible by $\bar G$; its quotient $w$ has degree below $e$. This constructs a preimage of $q$. If the image of $(v,w)$ is zero, reduction modulo $\bar G$ and invertibility of $\bar H$ there give $v=0$, by its degree bound, and monic multiplication then gives $w=0$. Thus this is an isomorphism even when $D$ has zero divisors. Degree-zero factors are covered by empty polynomial modules.

Consequently $\Delta$ has a unit value at the prescribed coefficient tuple. Set $C=(C_0)_\Delta$. The square Jacobian calculation AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1 gives formal smoothness, and there are no remaining differential coordinates. Theorem 2.2 of that lesson therefore gives formal unramifiedness. The finite equations and principal localization give finite presentation, so $C/A$ is étale. The coefficient tuple defines a $D$-algebra retraction $\sigma:E=C/IC\to D$ of its structural map.

We select exactly this section in the closed fibre. Let $L=\ker\sigma$. Finite algebra generators $x_i$ of $E/D$ give finite ideal generators $x_i-\sigma(x_i)$ for $L$: replace each variable by its constant value in a polynomial and telescope the difference one variable at a time. The map $$ \delta:E\longrightarrow L/L^2,\qquad x\longmapsto x-\sigma(x)\pmod {L^2} $$ is a $D$-derivation, with $E$ acting on $L/L^2$ through $\sigma$. To check products, expand $x=\sigma(x)+\ell$ and $y=\sigma(y)+m$ and discard $\ell m\in L^2$. Since $E/D$ is étale by base change, its differentials vanish by the same Theorem 2.2. The universal differential property makes $\delta=0$. Its restriction to $L$ is the quotient map, so $L=L^2$.

Choose finite ideal generators $\ell_i$ and write $\ell_i=\sum_j m_{ij}\ell_j$ with $m_{ij}\in L$. The adjugate identity of S01, Lemma 1.2 shows that $a=\det(1-M)$ annihilates $L$, while $a\equiv1\pmod L$. Put $p=1-a\in L$. Then $p\ell=\ell$ for every $\ell\in L$, so $p^2=p$ and $L=pE$. Inverting $1-p$ kills precisely $L$ and induces $E_{1-p}\cong E/L=D$, compatibly with its structural map. Lift $1-p$ to $h\in C$ and put $A'=C_h$. Its closed fibre is this very copy of $D$, and principal localization preserves finite presentation and étaleness by AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2 and Section 4. The universal polynomials in $A'[T]$ supply $G',H'$. If both degrees are zero, one can directly take $A'=A$ and both factors equal to one. ∎

Lemma F.116: lift idempotent upstairs

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07M4.

Suppose $A\to B$ is integral and $I\subset A$ is an ideal. Every idempotent $\bar e\in B/IB$ lifts to an idempotent of $B\otimes_A A'$ after a finitely presented étale map $A\to A'$ for which $A/I\to A'/IA'$ is an isomorphism.

Proof. Choose $y\in B$ reducing to $\bar e$. The determinant proof F.111 gives an integer $d\ge1$ and a monic $f\in A[T]$ with $$ f(y)=0,\qquad \bar f=T^d(T-1)^d. $$ The two factors generate the unit ideal: in the expansion of $(T+(1-T))^{2d-1}=1$, every term contains either $T^d$ or $(1-T)^d$. Apply F.115. Over its étale algebra $A_1$ we have $f=GH$ with reductions $T^d$ and $(T-1)^d$. Put $B_1=B\otimes_AA_1$, write $y_1$ for the image of $y$, and set $b_1=G(y_1)$, $b_2=H(y_1)$. Then $$ b_1b_2=0,\qquad \bar b_1=\bar e,\quad \bar b_2=(-1)^d(1-\bar e). $$ Thus $b_1,b_2$ generate the unit ideal modulo $IB_1$.

The map $A_1\to B_1$ remains integral. Indeed each tensor element uses finitely many elements of $B$; their monic equations generate a finite module algebra after base change, and its elements are integral by the determinant test AG-CA-05, Theorems 1.1–1.2. Let $K$ be the inverse image in $A_1$ of the ideal $(b_1,b_2)B_1$. The closed-image and lying-over proof in Theorem 3.4 of that lesson gives $$ \operatorname{image}V_{B_1}(b_1,b_2)=V_{A_1}(K). $$ No prime in this image can contain $IA_1$, since its prime upstairs would contain $IB_1$ as well as $b_1,b_2$. Hence $V(K+IA_1)$ is empty and $K+IA_1=A_1$, by the prime-separation proof AG-CA-01, Lemma 1.1. Choose $a\in K$ with $a\equiv1\pmod {IA_1}$ and set $A'=(A_1)_a$.

In $B'=B_1\otimes_{A_1}A'$, the image of $a$ is a unit belonging to $(b_1,b_2)$. Choose $u,v\in B'$ with $ub_1+vb_2=1$ and put $e'=ub_1$. The equations give $$ e'(1-e')=uvb_1b_2=0, $$ so $e'$ is idempotent. Reducing $ub_1+vb_2=1$ and multiplying by $\bar e$ gives $\bar u\bar e=\bar e$, proving that $e'$ reduces to the specified idempotent. Finally $a$ reduces to one, so the last localization leaves the quotient $A_1/IA_1=A/I$ unchanged. Its composition with $A\to A_1$ is finitely presented étale by the proved stability in AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2 and Section 4. This supplies every stated property, including the zero closed fibre. ∎

Lemma F.117: lift projective module

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 07M5.

For an ideal $I$ of any ring $A$ and a finite projective $A/I$-module $\bar P$, there is a finitely presented étale map $A\to A'$ inducing $A/I\cong A'/IA'$, and a finite projective $A'$-module $P'$ with $P'/IP'\cong\bar P$ under that identification.

Proof. Realize $\bar P$ as a direct summand of $(A/I)^n$ and let $\bar p$ be its projector. Such a realization follows from projectivity by splitting a finite free surjection, as in S01, Lemma 1.0. Lift the finitely many entries of $\bar p$ to a matrix $\varphi$ over $A$. Its characteristic polynomial $f(T)=\det(T1-\varphi)$ is monic. The full coefficient proof of Cayley–Hamilton F.19 gives an algebra map $$ B=A[T]/(f)\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_A(A^n), \qquad x\longmapsto\varphi, $$ where $x$ is the class of $T$. For $n>0$, subtracting the leading coefficient times the appropriate power of $T$ times the monic polynomial $f$ reduces any polynomial to degree below $n$. Conversely, for nonzero $q$, the leading coefficient of $qf$ equals that of $q$ and its degree is $\deg q+n$; thus no nonzero multiple of $f$ has degree below $n$. These two calculations show that $1,x,\ldots,x^{n-1}$ are a free $A$-basis of $B$, even when $A$ has zero divisors. The proved finite-algebra determinant criterion AG-CA-05, Theorem 1.2 now makes $A\to B$ integral. The case $n=0$ is handled directly below.

In each residue field of $A/I$, an idempotent linear operator decomposes the vector space into its image and kernel: $v=\bar p v+(1-\bar p)v$, and applying $\bar p$ proves the intersection zero. Choose bases of the two summands. Its characteristic polynomial there is $T^{n-r}(T-1)^r$ for the dimension $r$ of its image. Consequently at every prime of $B/IB$ the image of $x$ is zero or one: pass to the field of that prime and use this factorization. The nilradical calculation AG-CA-01, Theorem 1.2 then gives an integer $N\ge1$ such that $$ x^N(1-x)^N=0\quad\text{in }E=B/IB. $$ This uses a single nilpotent element, with no Noetherian condition.

Set $a=x^N$, $b=(1-x)^N$ in $E$. They generate the unit ideal: expand $(x+(1-x))^{2N-1}$, whose every term is divisible by $a$ or $b$. Also $ab=0$. Choose $u,v$ with $ua+vb=1$. Then $(a+b)(u^2a+v^2b)=u^2a^2+v^2b^2=(ua+vb)^2=1$. Thus $a+b$ is a unit, and $$ \epsilon=\frac{a}{a+b},\qquad \epsilon(1-\epsilon)=\frac{ab}{(a+b)^2}=0 $$ is an idempotent. Under the reduction of the displayed endomorphism map, $a$ goes to $\bar p^N=\bar p$, $b$ to $(1-\bar p)^N=1-\bar p$, and their sum to the identity. Hence $\epsilon$ maps to exactly $\bar p$.

Apply F.116 to the integral algebra $B/A$ and this idempotent of $B/IB$. It supplies the required étale $A'$ and an idempotent of $B\otimes_AA'$ lifting $\epsilon$. Its image in $\operatorname{End}_{A'}((A')^n)$ is a projector $p'$ reducing to $\bar p$. Put $P'=\operatorname{im}p'$. The decomposition $$ (A')^n=\operatorname{im}p'\oplus\operatorname{im}(1-p') $$ follows by writing each vector as the sum of its two projections; applying $p'$ makes their intersection zero. The projections of the finite coordinate basis generate each summand, so $P'$ is finite projective. Reduction preserves this split decomposition and identifies its first summand with $\operatorname{im}\bar p=\bar P$. If $n=0$, take $A'=A$ and $P'=0$ directly. This also handles $A/I=0$ by choosing its zero module with $n=0$. ∎

Lemma F.118: noetherian finite all equivalent

Reading source: Stacks, Tag 09CC, together with the regular-sequence and Koszul arguments cited there. The proof below is independently written for finite modules.

For a nonzero finite module over a Noetherian local ring and a list in its maximal ideal, regularity, vanishing of all positive Koszul homology, vanishing of first Koszul homology, and the polynomial associated-graded condition are equivalent.

Proof. Write $(A,\mathfrak m)$ for the ring, $M$ for the module, and $J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$. The fourth assertion means that the natural graded map $$\theta:(M/JM)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{n\geq0}J^nM/J^{n+1}M,\qquad \bar mT^a\longmapsto[mf^a],$$ is an isomorphism. It is always surjective. If $r=0$, the Koszul complex has only $M$ in degree zero, $J=0$, and $\theta$ is the identity in degree zero. The empty list is regular because $M\ne0$. Thus all four assertions hold in that case; assume $r>0$.

Use the exterior complex on the symbols $e_1,\ldots,e_r$, with coefficients in $M$, differential $d(e_i)=f_i$, and the signed product rule. Separating wedges which contain $e_r$ identifies it with the cone of multiplication by $f_r$ on the complex for the first $r-1$ entries. Its homology sequence contains $$H_1(K_{r-1})\xrightarrow{f_r}H_1(K_{r-1})\longrightarrow H_1(K_r)\longrightarrow H_0(K_{r-1})\xrightarrow{f_r}H_0(K_{r-1}).$$ For the two consequences needed here, exactness can also be checked directly. A degree-one cycle of $K_{r-1}$ becomes a boundary in $K_r$ when $H_1(K_r)=0$. Writing that boundary as the sum of a wedge without $e_r$ and a wedge containing $e_r$ shows that its class in $H_1(K_{r-1})$ is $f_r$ times a class represented by a cycle. This gives surjectivity of the first arrow. If $f_rm\in(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})M$, choose coefficients for this equality to obtain a degree-one cycle in $K_r$ with last coefficient $m$. A degree-two boundary has last coefficient in $(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})M$, so $[m]=0$ in $H_0(K_{r-1})$. This gives injectivity of the last arrow.

If $H_1(K_r)=0$, the preceding $H_1$ is a finite $A$-module, since its complex consists of finite modules over a Noetherian ring. Nakayama, with $f_r\in\mathfrak m$, makes it zero by the surjectivity just proved. Induction therefore gives all successive multiplication injections, including the final one displayed above. Their last quotient is nonzero by Nakayama applied to $M/JM$. This proves regularity. Conversely, assume the list regular and the preceding complex acyclic in positive degrees. A cycle in $K_r$ of degree $k$ has a component $v$ multiplying $e_r$, and $v$ is a cycle of degree $k-1$ in $K_{r-1}$. For $k\geq2$, preceding acyclicity makes $v$ a boundary. For $k=1$, the cycle identity says $f_r[v]=0$ in $H_0(K_{r-1})$; regularity again makes $v$ a boundary. Subtract the differential of a suitable wedge containing $e_r$ to remove $v$. What remains is a degree-$k$ cycle in $K_{r-1}$ and is a boundary by preceding acyclicity. This proves acyclicity in every positive degree by induction. In particular it implies vanishing of $H_1$.

We next prove that a regular list makes $\theta$ injective. In degree zero this is the defining quotient $M/JM$. In degree one, suppose $\sum_i f_im_i\in J^2M$. Express this element as $\sum_i f_iu_i$ with $u_i\in JM$, and subtract. The vector $(m_i-u_i)$ is a degree-one Koszul cycle. By the preceding acyclicity it is a boundary, whose coefficients all belong to $JM$, since the degree-two differential has coefficients $f_i$. Consequently every $m_i\in JM$. This proves directly the module version of the conormal calculation in F.74.

Here is a coefficient calculation for any degree $n\geq1$. In a relation $$\sum_{|a|=n}m_af^a\in J^{n+1}M,$$ collect every term involving one of $f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1}$ into their generated submodule. The only remaining term on the left is $m_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}f_r^n$; the only remaining type on the right is $u f_r^{n+1}$. Thus $$\bigl(m_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}-uf_r\bigr)f_r^n+\sum_{i<r}f_iv_i=0$$ for suitable $u,v_i\in M$. The list $f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},f_r^n$ is regular by AG-CA-12, Proposition 1.3, whose power argument applies to modules. Its first Koszul homology is zero by the cone argument. Hence the last coefficient of this relation belongs to $(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})M$, so $m_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}\in JM$.

To recover the coefficients of all monomials, put $B=A[U_1,\ldots,U_r,U_r^{-1}]$, $N=M\otimes_AB$, and $$g_i=f_i-(U_i/U_r)f_r\quad(i<r),\qquad g_r=f_r/U_r.$$ The ring $B$ is free and faithfully flat over $A$, with its Laurent monomials as a basis. Tensoring preserves Koszul acyclicity. The displayed change of generators is invertible, so its exterior powers identify the two Koszul complexes and give $H_1(K(g;N))=0$.

Fix a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $B$. If $N_{\mathfrak p}=0$, every term of every Koszul complex with these coefficients is zero. If $N_{\mathfrak p}\ne0$ and $JB\subset\mathfrak p$, the local criterion already proved makes $g_1,\ldots,g_r$ regular on the nonzero finite $B_{\mathfrak p}$-module $N_{\mathfrak p}$. Its power list $g_1,\ldots,g_{r-1},g_r^n$ is regular and has zero $H_1$. Finally, if $JB\not\subset\mathfrak p$, at least one $g_i$ is a unit in $B_{\mathfrak p}$. The power list still contains a unit, so choose $a_i$ with $\sum_{i<r}a_ig_i+a_rg_r^n=1$. Wedge multiplication by $\sum_i a_ie_i$ satisfies $dh+hd=1$ by the signed product rule, and contracts its Koszul complex. These three cases show that the power list has zero first homology at every prime. Localization commutes with the complex and its homology; a module whose localizations at all primes vanish is zero. The global $H_1$ therefore vanishes as well.

The preceding pure-last-coefficient calculation now applies to $g$ on $N$. Substituting $f_i=g_i+U_ig_r$ for $i<r$ and $f_r=U_rg_r$ makes the coefficient of $g_r^n$ equal to $\sum_{|a|=n}m_aU^a$. Thus this element belongs to $JN$. Since $N/JN=(M/JM)\otimes_AB$ is the direct sum of its Laurent monomial copies of $M/JM$, each coefficient $m_a$ belongs to $JM$. This proves injectivity of $\theta$ in every degree.

For the converse, suppose $\theta$ is an isomorphism. Krull intersection, AG-CA-03, Theorem 6.1, gives $\bigcap_{n\geq0}J^nM=0$. Every nonzero $m\in M$ therefore has a finite order $v$, characterized by $m\in J^vM\setminus J^{v+1}M$. Its initial class is nonzero; multiplication by $T_1$ is injective on $(M/JM)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]$, so $f_1m$ is nonzero and has order $v+1$. In particular $f_1$ acts injectively on $M$. The same calculation gives $$f_1M\cap J^nM=f_1J^{n-1}M\qquad(n\geq1):$$ if $f_1m\in J^nM$ and $m\ne0$, its order forces $m\in J^{n-1}M$; the reverse inclusion follows from $f_1\in J$.

Set $M'=M/f_1M$ and let $J'$ be the ideal induced by $J$. In degree $n\geq1$, the last equality identifies the kernel of $J^nM/J^{n+1}M\to J'^nM'/J'^{n+1}M'$ with multiplication by $T_1$ from degree $n-1$. Indeed an element in that kernel is $y+f_1m$, with $y\in J^{n+1}M$; then $f_1m\in J^nM$, so $m\in J^{n-1}M$. Degree zero is unchanged. It follows that $$\operatorname{gr}_{J'}M'\simeq(M/JM)[T_2,\ldots,T_r].$$ Repeat the order and quotient argument for the remaining entries. Nakayama ensures that each finite intermediate module and the final quotient are nonzero. This proves regularity and hence all four equivalences. ∎

Lemma F.119: p basis

Reading source: AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 11972–12025.

Let $L/F$ be a field extension of characteristic $p>0$ and put $E=FL^p$. A subset $C\subset L$ is $p$-independent over $F$ when its monomials, with finite support and exponents between $0$ and $p-1$, are linearly independent over $E$. It is a $p$-basis when those monomials are a basis of $L$ over $E$. Independence holds exactly when the differentials $dc$ are linearly independent over $L$ in $\Omega_{L/F}$. Every such subset extends to a $p$-basis. Moreover $C$ is a $p$-basis exactly when its differentials form an $L$-basis of $\Omega_{L/F}$.

Proof. All derivations over $F$ annihilate $E$: they kill $F$, the product rule kills $p$th powers, and the inverse rule kills the field generated by these elements. We first construct the coordinate system for a maximal $p$-independent set.

Order the $p$-independent supersets of the prescribed set by inclusion. A chain has an independent union, since any proposed relation involves finitely many elements contained together in one member of the chain. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal set $B$. For each finite $B_0\subset B$, the algebra $E[B_0]$ is spanned by its standard monomials, because $b^p\in E$. It is a finite-dimensional domain and therefore a field: multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective linear endomorphism, hence surjective, and its inverse image of one supplies an inverse. The union $E[B]$ is consequently a field as well.

Suppose $x\in L\setminus E[B]$. Its minimal polynomial over that field divides $T^p-x^p$. In $L[T]$ this polynomial is $(T-x)^p$, and unique Euclidean factorization shows that any monic divisor is $(T-x)^r$. If $0<r<p$ and this divisor were defined over $E[B]$, its next coefficient $-rx$ would put $x$ there, a contradiction. Thus the minimal polynomial has degree $p$. The power basis of this degree-$p$ extension, together with independence of the old monomials, proves that $B\cup\{x\}$ remains $p$-independent. Maximality rules this out, so $E[B]=L$.

There is now an exact presentation $$ L=E[T_b:b\in B]/(T_b^p-b^p:b\in B). $$ Surjectivity follows from $E[B]=L$. For injectivity, reduce a polynomial, which involves only finitely many variables, by the displayed monic relations. Its reduced standard-monomial expression can vanish only when every coefficient is zero, by $p$-independence. This proves the presentation for infinite sets too.

Differentiate polynomials in a single variable $T_b$, killing $E$ and all other variables. Each defining relation has derivative zero, so this operation descends through the exact presentation to an $F$-derivation $\partial_b:L\to L$.
